a: These are the names of the sons of Israel
p: The book's Hebrew title is Shemot, "Names." It opens with "and," as if Genesis had never stopped.
b: Jewish readers name each book of the Torah by an early word, so Exodus is Shemot, "Names." The first word is actually ve-elleh, "And these," tying the book to Genesis. The sentence nearly repeats Genesis 46:8, "These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt." The English title comes from the Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, which called the book Exodos, "the way out." So one title looks back to the family that went down to Egypt, and the other looks ahead to the people who come out. Luke uses the same Greek word when Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about the exodos he would complete at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31).

a: came from Jacob's body
p: The Hebrew says the seventy "came out of Jacob's thigh," a polite way to say they were his own offspring.
b: The phrase is yotse'e yerekh Ya'aqov, "those coming out of Jacob's thigh." "Thigh" is a modest word for the body's power to father children (compare the oath "under the thigh" in Genesis 24:2 and Judges 8:30, where Gideon's seventy sons "came out of his thigh"). Genesis 46:26 uses the same expression for the family that went down: "those who sprang from his own body." The point is that the whole nation which follows grows from one man's household.

a: the Israelites were fruitful and swarmed
t: Creation words for a growing people
p: Five verbs of growth echo God's first blessing in Genesis 1: Israel is doing what humans were made to do.
b: "Were fruitful," "swarmed," "grew many," "became strong" and "the land was filled" pile up the language of Genesis 1:28, "Be fruitful and grow many. Fill the earth." "Swarm" is the word used for the teeming water creatures of Genesis 1:20. The blessing given to Adam, to Noah (Genesis 9:1) and to Jacob (Genesis 35:11) is coming true in Egypt, and the promise to Abraham of countless offspring (Genesis 15:5; 22:17) is being kept. The same growth that shows God's blessing is what frightens Pharaoh in the next verses.
r: Genesis 1:20–22; Genesis 1:28; Genesis 9:1; Genesis 35:11; Genesis 47:27; Acts 7:17

a: a king who did not know Joseph
p: The text never names this Pharaoh. Candidates depend on when one dates the exodus.
b: Exodus names no Pharaoh, a habit that matches Egyptian usage before about 950 BC, when "Pharaoh" alone served as a title. Early-date readers (exodus about 1446 BC) often think of a king of the Eighteenth Dynasty, such as Ahmose, who drove out the Asiatic Hyksos rulers of the Delta, so a new native dynasty would have reason to fear Semites in the northeast. Late-date readers (exodus about 1260s BC) think of Seti I or Ramesses II, the builders of the city Rameses (1:11). The Talmud records Rav and Shmuel disagreeing: was he truly new, or the same king with new decrees, who acted "as if" he did not know Joseph? "Know" here means to acknowledge, to feel obligation.

a: go up from the land
p: Pharaoh fears the Israelites will "go up from the land": he wants their labor, and he fears losing it.
b: It seems odd that a king who fears a foreign people would worry that they might leave. The point is economic: Pharaoh wants the workforce. Rashi, following the Talmud, reads it as a man cursing himself under a cover phrase, meaning "and drive us out of the land." Either way the words are ironic. What Pharaoh most fears, Israel "going up" from Egypt, is exactly what the book will narrate (3:8; 13:18). His plan to prevent it brings it about.

a: let us outsmart them
p: Judith retells Pharaoh's plan with the same Greek verb the Septuagint uses here for "outsmart."
b: In the Greek Septuagint, Pharaoh's word is katasophizomai, "to deal cleverly." Judith, a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians include in the Old Testament, uses the same verb when Achior the Ammonite tells the Assyrian general the story of the Exodus: "They outwitted them and set them to hard labor and brick-making" (Judith 5:11). Achior's point is that Egypt's cleverness failed. Israel's God struck Egypt with plagues, and the Egyptians drove his people out (Judith 5:12). Achior means it as a warning to Assyria. Stephen uses the same verb for Pharaoh in Acts 7:19.

a: slave-gang bosses
p: Mas means state forced labor. Later, Solomon would put Israelites to the same kind of work.
b: Sare missim are "officers of forced labor." Mas is the corvée, work a state required of a conquered or subject population. Egypt used such labor for its building projects, and Egyptian texts speak of foreigners, including people called 'Apiru, hauling stone for royal works (Papyrus Leiden 348, from the reign of Ramesses II). The same word returns with a bitter twist when King Solomon puts a mas on Israel and Canaanites to build the temple and his palace (1 Kings 5:13; 9:15–21). The rebels of 1 Kings 12:4, 18 remember it.

a: Pithom and Rameses
p: Two real Delta cities. Rameses is usually Pi-Ramesse, the capital of Ramesses II, a key clue for dating the exodus.
b: Rameses is most often identified with Pi-Ramesse ("House of Ramesses"), the great Delta capital built by Ramesses II (reigned about 1279–1213 BC) at Qantir, beside the older Hyksos capital Avaris (Tell el-Dab'a). Many read this as evidence for a thirteenth-century exodus. Early-date scholars reply that the name may be updated, as in Genesis 47:11, where Joseph's family settles in "the land of Rameses" centuries before that king. Pithom is Egyptian Pi-Atum, "House of Atum," usually placed in the Wadi Tumilat at Tell el-Maskhuta or Tell er-Retaba. Donald Redford argued that Tell el-Maskhuta was occupied mainly from the 600s BC, pointing to a late writer; Hoffmeier and others favor Tell er-Retaba, occupied in the New Kingdom.

a: grew sick with fear
p: Quts mixes fear with disgust. The same word describes Moab's terror of Israel in Numbers 22:3.
b: Vayyaqutsu means they felt a sickened dread, a fear mixed with loathing. The word appears again when Moab "was sick with dread because of the Israelites" (Numbers 22:3), and when Rebekah says she is "sick of living" (Genesis 27:46). The Egyptians are not only afraid of the Hebrews; they come to see them as something foreign and repulsive, the attitude that makes cruelty easy.

a: in clay and bricks
p: Egyptian paintings show foreign workers making mud bricks, much as Exodus describes.
b: Most Egyptian buildings except temples and tombs were made of sun-dried mud brick, mixed with chopped straw (see 5:7). A painting in the tomb of the vizier Rekhmire at Thebes (about 1450 BC) shows workers, some of them Asiatic foreigners, hauling water, mixing clay, shaping bricks in molds and stacking them under the eye of overseers with sticks. Such scenes do not prove the exodus, since brickmaking was common, but they show that the details of chapters 1 and 5 fit the Egyptian world. Chomer can mean clay or mortar.

a: They turned their lives bitter
p: The verb for "made bitter" names the bitter herbs eaten at Passover (12:8).
b: Vaymareru, "they made bitter," shares its root with merorim, the bitter herbs of the Passover meal (12:8). Rabban Gamaliel's rule in the Mishnah (Pesachim 10:5), repeated in the Haggadah, explains each food: "bitter herbs, because the Egyptians embittered the lives of our fathers in Egypt," quoting this verse. At the Seder table the taste of horseradish or romaine is meant to put the eater back into this verse.

a: the Hebrew midwives
t: Hebrew midwives, or midwives to the Hebrews?
p: The Hebrew can mean midwives who were Hebrews or Egyptian midwives who served Hebrew women.
b: Ha-meyalledot ha-'ivriyyot most naturally means "the Hebrew midwives," and their names, Shiphrah ("beautiful") and Puah (perhaps "girl" or "splendid"), are Semitic. A name close to Shiphrah appears in a list of Semitic servants in an Egyptian papyrus of the 1700s BC (Brooklyn Papyrus 35.1446). But the phrase can also mean "midwives of the Hebrew women," and Josephus says plainly that they were Egyptians (Antiquities 2.206); the Septuagint's wording can be read that way too, which would make their fear of God (1:17) even more striking. The Talmud identifies them with Jochebed and Miriam. Two midwives for a nation is too few; they may have been the heads of a guild.

a: watch the two stones
p: Ovnayim, "the two stones," is probably a birthstool. Egyptian women gave birth crouching on bricks.
b: Ha-ovnayim is a dual form, "the pair of stones." Most scholars take it as the birthing stool: Egyptian women gave birth squatting on two bricks or stones, and Egyptian texts speak of the "birth bricks." In 2001 Josef Wegner excavated a painted birth brick at Abydos, showing a mother with her newborn. Jeremiah 18:3 uses the same word for a potter's wheel, with its two stone disks. Some rabbis read it as a polite word for the baby's body, so the midwives would check the child's sex. Either way the king wants the killing done at the moment of birth, quietly, by the women trusted to bring life.

a: But the midwives feared God
p: The midwives refuse a royal order and then mislead Pharaoh. Readers have praised and puzzled over both acts.
b: This is often called the first recorded act of civil disobedience. "Fearing God" in the Bible means a moral restraint that holds even where no human law does (Genesis 20:11; 42:18). Jewish tradition honors the midwives highly: the Talmud says they did more than refrain, they fed and cared for the babies. Christian readers have debated their answer in 1:19. Augustine (Against Lying) argued that God rewarded their mercy, not their lie, and that they would have done better to tell the truth; Calvin took a similar line. Many modern readers, citing Rahab (Joshua 2), think deceiving a murderer to save life is not the sin forbidden by the commandment against false witness.

a: They are full of life
p: Chayot can mean "lively" or "like animals." The midwives may be playing on Pharaoh's contempt.
b: Chayot is a rare adjective from the root "live." It may mean "vigorous," quick to give birth. The same letters spell chayyot, "animals," and the Talmud and Rashi take it that way: the Hebrew women give birth like animals in the field, without help. If so, the midwives are telling Pharaoh exactly what a man who despises the Hebrews would like to believe. The word also fits the chapter's theme: Pharaoh orders death, and the Hebrew women are full of life.

a: he made households for them
p: God "made houses" for the midwives: families of their own, or, in Jewish tradition, the priestly and royal houses.
b: "Houses" here means families, descendants. The pronoun lahem is masculine, which can happen with feminine groups in Hebrew but has led to other readings. Rashi, following the Talmud, says God gave the midwives "houses" of priesthood and kingship, since he takes them to be Jochebed (mother of Moses and Aaron) and Miriam (whom tradition makes an ancestor of David). A few modern readers take "he" as Pharaoh, who "made houses" to watch the Hebrews, but most take God as the subject.

a: you must throw into the Nile
p: Pharaoh drowns Hebrew boys in the Nile; in the end Egypt's army drowns in the sea.
b: The decree moves from secret to public: now every Egyptian is to take part. Readers have long noticed how the story answers it. The one boy saved from the Nile becomes the man who leads Israel through the sea in which Egypt's army drowns (14:28; 15:4). The Wisdom of Solomon makes the link explicit: because the Egyptians resolved to kill the infants, God "destroyed them all together by a mighty flood" (Wisdom 18:5). Christians have also compared Herod's killing of Bethlehem's boys and the escape of the child Jesus (Matthew 2:13–18).

a: A man from Levi's family
p: Moses' parents are not named until 6:20. The story keeps its focus on what happens, not on pedigree.
b: The man and woman stay unnamed here; we learn later that they are Amram and Jochebed, and that Jochebed was Amram's aunt (6:20). The withholding fits a chapter in which almost no one is named except the baby. It also creates a puzzle: Moses has an older sister (2:4) and an older brother, Aaron (7:7), yet this verse sounds like a first marriage. The Talmud (Sotah 12a) solves it by saying Amram had divorced his wife because of Pharaoh's decree, and Miriam talked him into remarrying her. Most modern readers simply take the verse as the start of a new story.

a: She saw him, that he was good
p: The words echo God seeing that the light was good in Genesis 1. A new beginning is starting.
b: "She saw him, that he was good" (va-tere oto ki tov hu) matches the refrain of creation: "God saw the light, that it was good" (Genesis 1:4). Most versions say "a fine child" or "beautiful," and Stephen calls him "beautiful before God" (Acts 7:20), as does Hebrews 11:23. The Talmud (Sotah 12a) says that when Moses was born the whole house was filled with light. The narrator invites the reader to see more than a mother's pride: in a land of death, something new and good has been made.

a: a papyrus ark
t: Not a basket but an ark
p: Tevah, the word for the baby's box, is used elsewhere only for Noah's ark. The link is hidden by "basket."
b: Tevah appears in the Bible only here (2:3, 5) and in Genesis 6–9 for Noah's ark. Both are boxes sealed against water, both carry a chosen life through waters of death, and both stories begin a new chapter of God's work. "Basket" is a fair description of a papyrus container, but it hides the echo, so the Plain English keeps "ark." The word is probably borrowed from Egyptian db3t, "box, coffin." Papyrus boats were used on the Nile (Isaiah 18:2).

a: smeared it with tar and pitch
p: An Akkadian legend tells of a king set adrift as a baby in a sealed reed basket. Is Moses' story borrowed?
b: The "Legend of Sargon," known from Neo-Assyrian copies of about the 700s BC, has the great king of Akkad (about 2300 BC) say that his mother, a priestess, "set me in a basket of rushes, she sealed my lid with bitumen, she cast me into the river," where Aqqi the water-drawer lifted him out and raised him. Brian Lewis collected dozens of similar "exposed hero" stories from many cultures. Many critical scholars think Exodus uses this widespread motif. Conservative scholars note that abandoning infants was a real practice, and that the differences are large: Moses' mother acts to save him, not to be rid of him, and the story turns the motif upside down, since a slave's child is raised as royalty. A shared motif is likely; direct copying is not proven.

a: in the reeds
p: Suf, "reeds," is the same word as in Yam Suf, the Sea of Reeds. Moses is saved where Israel will be saved.
b: The ark is set among the suf, the reeds or rushes along the bank. The same word names the sea Israel will cross: Yam Suf, "the Sea of Reeds" (10:19; 13:18; 15:4). The child is drawn out of the waters among the suf, and the nation will be brought through the waters of the Yam Suf. Jonah 2:5 uses suf for the seaweed wrapped around the drowning prophet.

a: Pharaoh's daughter
p: Exodus does not name her. Josephus calls her Thermuthis; rabbinic tradition calls her Bithiah.
b: Josephus names her Thermuthis (Antiquities 2.224), and Jubilees 47:5 calls her Tharmuth. Rabbinic tradition identifies her with "Bithiah, daughter of Pharaoh" in 1 Chronicles 4:18, whose name was read as Bat-Yah, "daughter of the LORD": she was honored as a woman who left her father's idols. Popular books on the early date suggest Hatshepsut, the famous queen of the 1400s BC, but there is no evidence for this. A royal daughter bathing in the Nile, which Egyptians regarded as sacred and life-giving, is plausible in any period.

a: sent her slave woman
p: Amatah means "her slave woman," but the rabbis also read it as "her arm," stretched out to reach the ark.
b: The plain sense of amatah is "her slave woman." Written without vowels, the same letters can be read ammatah, "her forearm." The Talmud (Sotah 12b) and Rashi record the reading that Pharaoh's daughter stretched out her own arm, which miraculously lengthened to reach the ark. The midrash makes her personally responsible for the rescue, which the next verse supports: she herself opens the ark, sees the child and pities him.

a: Her heart went out to him
t: The women who save the savior
p: Five women defy Pharaoh's decree in chapters 1–2: two midwives, a mother, a sister and Pharaoh's own daughter.
b: Pharaoh told his people to drown the boys and let the daughters live (1:22). He feared the wrong sex. J. Cheryl Exum showed how the daughters he spared undo his plan: Shiphrah and Puah, Moses' mother, his sister, and Pharaoh's own daughter, who knows he is a Hebrew child and saves him anyway. The verb chamal, "pity, spare," is the turning point. Jewish tradition counts Pharaoh's daughter among the righteous of the nations. Feminist and liberation readers see these women as the true beginning of the exodus, before Moses does anything.

a: the young woman went off
p: Miriam is called an almah, the same word used in Isaiah 7:14. It means a young woman, a girl near marrying age.
b: Ha-'almah is Moses' sister, probably Miriam (15:20), here a girl old enough to be sent on an errand and to speak to a princess. The word means a young woman, usually unmarried; it is used of Rebekah at the well (Genesis 24:43) and in the famous sign of Isaiah 7:14, which the Septuagint translated parthenos, "virgin," and Matthew 1:23 quotes. Jewish and critical readers point out that betulah is the more specific word for "virgin"; Christian readers reply that betulah is not always specific either (Joel 1:8) and that almah is never used of a married woman. See Isaiah 7:14.

a: From the water I drew him
p: Hebrew explains Moshe as "one who draws out." Egyptian -mose, "born," as in Thutmose, may be the real source.
b: The princess explains Moshe from the Hebrew verb mashah, "draw out" (only here and 2 Samuel 22:17 / Psalm 18:16). Strictly, Moshe is an active form, "the one who draws out," which fits his future better than his past: he will draw Israel out of the water (Isaiah 63:11). Most scholars think the name is Egyptian, from ms, "born, son," seen in Ahmose, Thutmose and Ramesses ("Ra is the one who bore him"), perhaps with a god's name dropped. The Bible then gives it a Hebrew meaning, as it often does with names. Josephus and Philo explained it from Egyptian mo, "water."

a: he went out to his brothers
p: The New Testament reads this as Moses' choice to side with Israel instead of Egypt's court.
b: Exodus says only that Moses "went out to his brothers" and "looked at their heavy labor," the same word for their burdens as in 1:11. Stephen adds that Moses was "educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians" and was forty years old (Acts 7:22–23). Hebrews 11:24–26 reads the moment as faith: he "would not be known as the son of Pharaoh's daughter," choosing to suffer with God's people. The repeated "his brothers" (twice in this verse) shows where his loyalty lies.

a: He turned this way and that and saw no one there
p: Readers have defended the killing as rescue, condemned it as murder, or called it right but premature.
b: The narrator does not judge. Jewish tradition mostly defends Moses: Exodus Rabbah says he "saw that there was no man" meaning no one of worth would come from the Egyptian, or no one else would act, and some midrashim say he killed by speaking God's name. Christian readers are divided. Stephen presents it as a rescue that Israel failed to understand (Acts 7:24–25). Augustine compared it to Peter cutting off the servant's ear: good zeal acting without authority. Many modern readers note that Moses looks around and hides the body, signs that he knew he would be blamed, and that God gives him forty years in the desert before calling him.

a: Who put you as a chief and a judge over us?
p: Stephen quotes this question in Acts 7 as a pattern: Israel first rejects the deliverer God sends.
b: The man's sneer is quoted twice by Stephen (Acts 7:27, 35): "This Moses whom they rejected... God sent as ruler and redeemer." Stephen uses it as a pattern, also seen in Joseph's story, of a deliverer first refused by his own people and later sent to save them, and applies it to Jesus. Jesus himself echoes the question when he refuses to settle an inheritance dispute: "Man, who put me in charge as judge or divider over you?" (Luke 12:14).

a: the land of Midian
p: Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba in northwest Arabia. Its people descended from Abraham's son Midian.
b: The Midianites were desert and oasis people of northwest Arabia, east of the Gulf of Aqaba, though their herders ranged into Sinai and the Negev. Genesis makes Midian a son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2), so Moses flees to distant relatives. Archaeologists link them with a painted pottery style found at Qurayyah and in the Timna copper mines, where a small tent shrine of the 1100s BC has been associated with Midianites. Midian later becomes Israel's enemy (Numbers 31; Judges 6–8), but here it is a refuge, and its priest becomes Moses' father-in-law and adviser (18:1–27).

a: he sat down by the well
p: Abraham's servant, Jacob and Moses all meet a future wife at a well. Readers expect what comes next.
b: Robert Alter called this a biblical "type-scene," a repeated pattern that readers would recognize. A man travels to a foreign land, meets a girl or girls at a well, someone draws water, the girls run home to tell, and a betrothal follows. Compare Rebekah in Genesis 24:10–27 and Rachel in Genesis 29:1–14. Each version shows something of the man: Jacob rolls away the stone, Moses drives off bullying shepherds and "saves" the women. The pattern returns, changed, in John 4, where Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well.

a: save them
p: Yasha, "save," is the verb later used when the LORD saves Israel at the sea (14:30).
b: Vayyoshi'an, "he saved them," comes from the root yasha, the Bible's main word for rescue, the root of the names Joshua and Jesus (Yehoshua, "the LORD saves"). Moses has twice stepped in for the weak: for a Hebrew against an Egyptian (2:12), and now for foreign women against shepherds. The daughters still call him "an Egyptian man" (2:19). The story prepares the reader for the great saving act, when "on that day the LORD saved Israel" (14:30).

a: Reuel
p: Moses' father-in-law has several names. Readers explain this by titles, by two generations, or by different sources.
b: He is Reuel here (also Numbers 10:29), Jethro in 3:1 and chapter 18, Jether in 4:18, and possibly Hobab in Judges 4:11, though Numbers 10:29 makes Hobab the son of Reuel. Traditional answers: Rashi says Reuel was the girls' grandfather, since "children call their grandfather 'father'" (on 2:18, and on Numbers 10:29 following the Sifre), and elsewhere that Jethro had seven names (on 18:1); others think Reuel was a clan name and Jethro ("excellence") a title. Source critics assign Reuel to the Yahwist (J) and Jethro to the Elohist (E), two traditions that remembered him differently.

a: Gershom
p: Gershom sounds like ger sham, "a foreigner there." Moses names his son for his own homelessness.
b: The name is explained from ger, "resident foreigner," and sham, "there." (The actual root may be garash, "drive out," which also fits a man driven from Egypt.) Moses, raised as an Egyptian, a Hebrew by birth, now living in Midian, is at home nowhere. The word ger becomes central to Israel's law: "You know the life of a foreigner from the inside, because you were foreigners living in the land of Egypt" (23:9). Abraham used the same word of himself (Genesis 23:4), and God told him his offspring would be ger in a land not theirs (Genesis 15:13).

a: God remembered his covenant
p: In Hebrew, to remember is to act on a commitment, not to recall something forgotten.
b: Zakhar, "remember," often means to turn one's attention to someone and act for them: "God remembered Noah" and the waters went down (Genesis 8:1); "God remembered Rachel" and she conceived (Genesis 30:22). Four verbs in 2:24–25 pile up God's attention: he heard, remembered, saw and knew. The covenant in view is God's promise to Abraham: "your offspring will be foreigners in a land that is not theirs... But I will judge the nation they serve, and afterward they will come out with great wealth" (Genesis 15:13–14).

a: the priest of Midian
t: Did Israel learn the LORD's name from Midian?
p: The "Midianite-Kenite hypothesis" says the worship of the LORD came from the south, through Moses' father-in-law.
b: Several old poems say the LORD "came from Sinai" or "from Seir," "from Teman," with Midian nearby (Deuteronomy 33:2; Judges 5:4; Habakkuk 3:3, 7). Egyptian lists from Soleb (Amenhotep III, 1300s BC) and Amarah-West (Ramesses II) mention "the land of the Shasu (nomads) of yhw," probably in that southern region. Many critical scholars therefore hold that the LORD was first worshiped by Midianite or Kenite groups and that Moses learned of him there. Traditional readers answer that Exodus presents the LORD as the God of Abraham long before (3:6), that Jethro confesses the LORD's greatness only after the exodus (18:11), and that a southern place name for the LORD's mountain fits the story as told.

a: past the edge of the wilderness
p: Achar ha-midbar is literally "behind the wilderness": the far side of it, or its western side.
b: Hebrew speakers oriented themselves facing east, so "behind" (achar) can mean "west" (Isaiah 9:12, where Philistines are "behind"). The phrase may mean that Moses led the flock to the far, remote side of the grazing land, or to its west. Shepherds moved flocks long distances in the dry season to find pasture, so the detail is natural.

a: God's mountain, toward Horeb
t: Where is the mountain of God?
p: Horeb and Sinai name the same mountain. Its location is unknown; at least a dozen sites have been proposed.
b: Exodus uses both "Horeb" (3:1; 17:6; 33:6) and "Sinai" (19:11), and Deuteronomy prefers Horeb; source critics assign the names to different traditions. The traditional site is Jebel Musa in southern Sinai, venerated by Christian monks by the 300s AD (the pilgrim Egeria visited about AD 383) and home to St. Catherine's Monastery since the 500s. Other proposals include Jebel Serbal, Har Karkom in the Negev (Emmanuel Anati), sites in northern Sinai, and Jebel al-Lawz in Saudi Arabia, favored by some because Paul places "Mount Sinai in Arabia" (Galatians 4:25), though "Arabia" in Paul's day included the Sinai and the Nabatean lands. Hoffmeier surveys the options.

a: The angel of the LORD appeared to him
p: The angel of the LORD appears, but then the LORD and God speak from the bush. Who is in the fire?
b: The text slides from "the angel of the LORD" (3:2) to "the LORD saw" and "God called" (3:4), as in Genesis 16:7–13 and 22:11–12. Jewish readers generally take the angel as God's messenger who carries his presence and speaks in his name; Exodus Rabbah names Michael or Gabriel. Christian writers from Justin Martyr (Dialogue 59–60) on saw the eternal Word, the Son, appearing before his incarnation, since Stephen calls him an angel and yet the voice says "I am the God of your ancestors" (Acts 7:30–32). Critical scholars often think "angel" was added to soften a direct appearance of God.

a: LORD
p: "LORD" in capitals stands for YHWH, the name God reveals to Moses in this chapter.
b: Wherever this translation prints "the LORD" in small capitals, the Hebrew has the four letters YHWH, God's personal name. "Lord" in ordinary letters translates Adonai, "my Lord" (as in 4:10). Jews out of reverence do not pronounce the name, reading Adonai or saying HaShem, "the Name." Most scholars think it was pronounced Yahweh, a form supported by Greek writers such as Clement of Alexandria (Iaoue). "Jehovah" comes from reading the four letters with the vowels of Adonai, a form that appeared in the late Middle Ages. Exodus 3:14–15 links the name to the verb hayah, "to be."

a: a thornbush
p: Seneh is a thorny desert shrub. Its sound recalls Sinai, the mountain where the bush grew.
b: Seneh occurs only here and in Deuteronomy 33:16, "the one who lived in the bush." It is probably a bramble or thorny acacia, common in the Sinai. The word sounds like Sinai, and many think the mountain's name and the bush are meant to recall each other. The Midrash (Exodus Rabbah 2:5) asks why God spoke from a lowly thornbush and not a great tree, and answers: to show that he shares Israel's pain, "I am at his side in hard times" (Psalm 91:15). Jesus refers to this passage as "the bush" (Mark 12:26).

a: the bush was not being eaten up
p: The bush that burns without burning up has stood for Israel, for the church and for Mary, mother of Jesus.
b: Jewish readers from Philo (Life of Moses 1.67) on have seen Israel in the bush: afflicted in the fire of Egypt but not destroyed. Protestant churches in Scotland and France took it as their emblem, with mottoes such as Nec tamen consumebatur, "yet it was not consumed." Eastern Orthodox and Catholic tradition, following Gregory of Nyssa (Life of Moses 2.21), read it as Mary, who bore God without being destroyed; there is an icon called "the Unburnt Bush." Some writers have offered natural explanations (a gas plant, desert light), but the text presents a sign: fire that does not need fuel, like the God who needs nothing to live.

a: "Moses! Moses!" He answered, "Here I am."
p: God calls Abraham, Jacob, Moses and Samuel with a doubled name, and each answers "Here I am."
b: The double call marks a turning point. At Mount Moriah "the angel of the LORD called to him from the sky: 'Abraham! Abraham!' He answered, 'Here I am'" (Genesis 22:11). God calls "Jacob, Jacob" before he goes down to Egypt (Genesis 46:2), and "Samuel! Samuel!" at Shiloh (1 Samuel 3:10). Hineni, "Here I am," is the answer of someone ready to listen and obey. Jesus uses the doubled name with Martha, Simon and Saul (Luke 10:41; 22:31; Acts 9:4).
r: Genesis 22:1; Genesis 22:11; Genesis 46:2; 1 Samuel 3:10; Isaiah 6:8; Acts 9:4

a: Pull your sandals off your feet
p: Taking off shoes before something holy is an old custom, kept in temples, mosques and many homes.
b: Joshua receives the same command before the commander of the LORD's army (Joshua 5:15). Exodus never lists shoes among the priests' garments (28:1–43), and Jewish tradition holds that the priests served barefoot in the temple. Removing sandals showed respect and humility, and left behind the dust of ordinary ground. The Qur'an retells this moment: "Take off your shoes: you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa" (Surah 20:12). The place is holy not because of the ground but because God is present there.

a: he was afraid to gaze at God
p: Moses hides his face. Later he will ask to see God's glory and be told no one can see his face and live.
b: This first fear prepares for a theme running through Exodus. At Sinai the elders "saw the God of Israel" (24:10), the LORD speaks with Moses "face to face" (33:11), and yet God says, "You cannot see my face, for no human being can see me and stay alive" (33:20). Jesus quotes this verse, "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob," to argue for the resurrection: God is not the God of the dead but of the living (Mark 12:26–27).

a: I have seen, yes seen
p: The Hebrew doubles the verb "see" for emphasis. God has looked closely at Israel's misery.
b: Ra'oh ra'iti uses the Hebrew infinitive with the verb, a common way of stressing an action: "I have truly seen." Three verbs follow: I have seen, I have heard, I know. The last, "I know their pains," is personal. Terence Fretheim and others see here a God who is affected by his people's suffering, not distant from it. Stephen quotes the verse almost word for word (Acts 7:34).

a: I have come down
p: God "comes down" to see Babel and Sodom, and here to rescue. Christians hear an echo of the incarnation.
b: The Bible often speaks of God "coming down" to act on earth: to see the tower of Babel (Genesis 11:5, 7), to look into Sodom (Genesis 18:21), and later onto Mount Sinai in fire (19:20). Here he comes down not to judge his people but to snatch them out of Egypt's hand. Christian readers connect this with Jesus' words, "I have come down from heaven" (John 6:38), and with the hymn of Philippians 2:6–8.

a: a land flowing with milk and honey
p: The milk is mostly from goats; the honey may be date syrup or bees' honey. Together they mean rich pasture.
b: This is the first of about twenty uses of the phrase. Milk came from goats and sheep grazing on good pasture. Devash can mean bees' honey (Judges 14:8) or a sweet syrup of dates or figs, which is how later rabbis read it. A large apiary of about 900 BC, with clay beehives, was found at Tel Rehov in the Jordan Valley. The phrase pictures a land rich for herders, not necessarily for farmers. A similar image appears in an Ugaritic poem, where the wadis run with honey when the god Baal lives again.
orig: אֶרֶץ זָבַת חָלָב וּדְבָשׁ (erets zavat chalav u-devash)
r: 3:17; 13:5; 33:3; Numbers 13:27; Deuteronomy 26:9; Jeremiah 11:5; Ezekiel 20:6; Jeremiah 16:14–15; Jeremiah 23:7–8; Micah 7:15

a: Who am I to go to Pharaoh?
p: Moses raises five objections (3:11; 3:13; 4:1; 4:10; 4:13). Prophets' calls often follow this pattern.
b: Moses objects that he is nobody (3:11), that he does not know God's name (3:13), that the people will not believe him (4:1), that he is no speaker (4:10), and finally simply asks God to send someone else (4:13). Norman Habel described a "call narrative" form shared with Gideon (Judges 6:11–24), Isaiah (Isaiah 6) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:4–10): a meeting with God, a commission, an objection, a reassurance, and a sign. Jewish tradition praised Moses' humility (Numbers 12:3); others see real reluctance and fear. God's answer to every objection begins with himself: "I will be with you."

a: Because I will be with you
p: God's answer uses ehyeh, "I will be," the very word he will soon give as his name (3:14).
b: Moses asks "Who am I?" and God does not answer the question; he tells Moses who will be with him. Ehyeh 'immakh, "I will be with you," anticipates 3:14, Ehyeh asher ehyeh. The same promise goes to Isaac (Genesis 26:3), Jacob (Genesis 31:3), Joshua (Joshua 1:5), Gideon (Judges 6:16), and in the New Testament the risen Jesus says, "I myself am with you every day" (Matthew 28:20). The sign that follows is strange: it can only be seen after Moses obeys.

a: you will all serve God on this mountain
t: From serving Pharaoh to serving God
p: Avad means both "to work as a slave" and "to worship." Exodus moves Israel from one service to the other.
b: The verb 'avad and the noun 'avodah appear again and again in Exodus. Israel "serves" Egypt with hard labor (1:13–14; 2:23); God demands, "Let my people go, so they may serve me" (4:23; 7:16; 8:1); and the book ends with the 'avodah of the tabernacle (35:24; 39:42). Many translations write "worship" when the object is God, which hides the play. Exodus does not picture Israel freed from all service, but changing masters: from Pharaoh, who crushes, to the LORD, who gives life. Stephen merges this verse with God's promise to Abraham: "After these things they will come out and serve me in this place" (Acts 7:7).

a: What is his name?
p: Did the Israelites not know God's name? Readers answer in very different ways.
b: In Genesis people already call on "the name of the LORD" (Genesis 4:26; 12:8). So why would the Israelites ask? Traditional answers: they had forgotten it in Egypt; or the question "what" (mah) asks what the name means, what this God is like and can do (Martin Buber, Moberly); or it tests whether Moses really met God. Source critics answer that in the Elohist (E) and Priestly (P) sources God's personal name is first revealed to Moses (compare 6:3), while the Yahwist (J) used it from the start. Both readings agree that the name is about to receive new meaning.

a: I will be who I will be
p: The famous answer can mean "I am who I am," "I will be who I will be," or "I am the one who is."
b: Ehyeh is the first-person form of hayah, "to be, become, be present." The Hebrew form usually points to ongoing or future action, so this translation says "I will be," linking it to "I will be with you" (3:12). Rashi, following the Talmud (Berakhot 9b), reads: "I will be with them in this trouble as I will be with them in later troubles." The Septuagint has egō eimi ho ōn, "I am the one who is," which Philo, the church fathers and Thomas Aquinas read as God's self-existence. The KJV has "I AM THAT I AM" and most modern versions "I am who I am," which some read as a refusal to be pinned down. W. F. Albright and Frank Cross proposed a causative sense, "he causes to be." All the readings may be heard at once. The Jewish Publication Society's NJPS leaves Ehyeh-Asher-Ehyeh untranslated, with "I Will Be What I Will Be" in its note.

a: I Will Be has sent me to you
p: Christians hear this verse in Jesus' words "Before Abraham came to be, I am" and in Revelation's "who is and who was."
b: In John 8:58 Jesus says, "Before Abraham came to be, I am," and his hearers pick up stones, apparently hearing a claim to the divine name. John's Gospel uses "I am" (egō eimi) alone several times (John 8:24, 28; 13:19; 18:5–6), echoing both this verse in Greek and Isaiah's "I am he" (Isaiah 43:10). Revelation names God "the one who is, who was, and who is coming" (Revelation 1:4, 8), a phrase that also appears in an expanded form in the Aramaic Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Deuteronomy 32:39. Jewish readers do not read these texts as pointing to Jesus, and many scholars think John draws mainly on Isaiah.
r: John 8:24; John 8:58; John 18:5–6; Isaiah 43:10; Revelation 1:4; Revelation 1:8; Revelation 4:8

a: This is my name for all time
p: The Talmud read le'olam, "forever," as le'allem, "to conceal," one root of the custom of not saying the name.
b: In the Hebrew text le'olam is written without its usual vowel letter, so it can be read le'allem, "to be hidden." The Talmud (Pesachim 50a) draws the lesson: "This is my name to be concealed, and this is how I am to be remembered": the name is written one way and spoken another. By the time of Jesus the name was spoken only in the Temple, by the priests in the priestly blessing and by the high priest on the Day of Atonement (Mishnah, Sotah 7:6; Yoma 6:2), and the Mishnah warns against pronouncing it as it is written (Sanhedrin 10:1). The second half, "by this name people will call me to mind," uses zekher, the name spoken in worship.

a: I have surely come to help you
p: God speaks the very words of Joseph's dying promise: "God will surely come to help you" (Genesis 50:24).
b: Paqod paqadti repeats the doubled verb of Genesis 50:24–25, where Joseph told his brothers, "God will surely come to help you, and he will bring you up from this land." Paqad means to visit, attend to, take note of; when God "visits" in this sense, he intervenes. The Midrash (Exodus Rabbah) says the elders believed Moses because Joseph had handed down this very phrase as the sign of the true redeemer. Moses will carry Joseph's bones out (13:19).

a: let us make a three days' journey into the wilderness
t: A three-day trip, or a trick?
p: God tells Moses to ask for only three days. Was this honest, a test, or a ruse?
b: Moses never asks Pharaoh outright for permanent freedom until much later. Some readers see a legitimate, small first request: if Pharaoh will not grant even this, his hardness is exposed (Sarna, Childs). Others see a deliberate ruse, part of the trickster theme in which the weak outwit the strong, like the midwives (Propp). Medieval Jewish commentators debated it too. "Three days" was a common distance for a festival or a meeting with God (Genesis 22:4; 19:11). Pharaoh himself later suspects the plan (10:10). The verb here is niqrah, "has met with us"; in 5:3 the Hebrew spells it niqra, as if from "call," a small spelling point the rabbis noticed.

a: except under a strong hand
p: The Hebrew can mean Pharaoh lets them go only when forced, or that not even force will move him.
b: Ve-lo be-yad chazaqah literally reads "and not by a strong hand." The Septuagint and Vulgate take it as "except by a strong hand," the sense most modern versions follow. The KJV reads "no, not by a mighty hand": even the plagues will not move Pharaoh, only the final blow. Both senses fit the story. "Strong hand" (yad chazaqah) shares its root with chazaq, the word used for Pharaoh's "stubborn" heart: two kinds of strength will meet.

a: Each woman will ask her neighbor
p: The KJV says Israel "borrowed" Egypt's silver and gold. The Hebrew sha'al means "ask for."
b: Sha'al means "ask, request." The KJV's "borrow" made it sound as if Israel took loans it never meant to repay, a charge used by critics of the Bible from ancient times. The text presents gifts given willingly by Egyptians who now "look kindly" on Israel (3:21; 12:36), fulfilling God's word that Abraham's offspring would "come out with great wealth" (Genesis 15:14). Ancient interpreters called them back wages: Philo, Jubilees and Tertullian (Against Marcion 2.20) say so, and the Talmud (Sanhedrin 91a) tells of a Jew who answered Egypt's claim before Alexander the Great by asking for the wages of 600,000 workers for 430 years. Augustine made "spoiling the Egyptians" a picture of Christians using pagan learning (On Christian Teaching 2.40).

a: What is that in your hand?
p: The Hebrew writes "what is this" as one word, mazzeh. Rashi heard "from this": a rebuke hidden in the question.
b: The standard Hebrew text writes mah-zeh, "what is this," as a single word, mazzeh (one of the spelling differences the scribes marked). Rashi, following the Midrash, read it as mi-zeh, "from this": with this very staff you deserve to be struck, for doubting God's people. The plain sense is simpler. God begins with what Moses already holds, an ordinary shepherd's staff, and makes it "the staff of God" (4:20).

a: it became a snake
p: Pharaohs wore a rearing cobra on their crowns. Moses grabs a snake by the tail: Egypt's power in his hand.
b: The uraeus, a rearing cobra, was the emblem of royal and divine power on the Pharaoh's crown, said to spit fire at his enemies. Many scholars see a message in this sign: the God of Israel can turn a shepherd's staff into Egypt's royal emblem and back, and puts it in Moses' hand. Catching a snake by the tail is the dangerous way to do it, so obeying the command took courage. In 7:9–12 a different word, tannin, is used for Aaron's staff.

a: struck with a skin disease, like snow
p: Tsara'at is a skin disease, not the modern leprosy. And the Hebrew says "like snow," not "white as snow."
b: Metsora'at describes tsara'at, the scaly or flaky skin condition regulated in Leviticus 13–14, which also could affect cloth and walls. It is not Hansen's disease (modern leprosy), which is not clearly attested in the Near East until much later. Many versions add "white," but the Hebrew says only "like snow" (ka-shaleg), probably meaning flaky. The same phrase describes Miriam (Numbers 12:10) and Gehazi (2 Kings 5:27). The sign shows that God can strike and heal; it may also hint that the hand Moses used to kill the Egyptian is in God's power.

a: the voice of the first sign
p: The Hebrew speaks of the "voice" of a sign: a sign is a message, something that speaks.
b: Most translations smooth the phrase into "the evidence" or "the message" of the sign, but Hebrew says qol ha-ot, "the voice of the sign." An ot is a token that points beyond itself: the rainbow (Genesis 9:12), circumcision (Genesis 17:11), the Sabbath (31:13), the blood on the doors (12:13). The three signs of chapter 4 are meant to speak for Moses, who fears he cannot speak.

a: I am heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue
t: Did Moses have a speech problem?
p: "Heavy of mouth" may mean a stammer, a lack of eloquence, or rusty Egyptian. Readers disagree.
b: Kevad peh u-khevad lashon literally means "heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue." A famous midrash (Exodus Rabbah 1:26) says the baby Moses, tested by Pharaoh, reached for a burning coal instead of gold and burned his tongue. Rashbam suggests he had lost his fluency in Egyptian after years in Midian. Others think he simply was not a gifted speaker, or that he is making excuses. Stephen says Moses "had power in his words and in his actions" (Acts 7:22). The word kaved, "heavy," will soon describe Pharaoh's heart (7:14): a heavy tongue and a heavy heart face each other.

a: Or who makes someone mute, or deaf, or sighted, or blind?
p: God claims to make people mute, deaf, seeing or blind. Readers wrestle with what that means.
b: God's reply answers Moses' weakness by pointing to the Creator. The verse is often discussed in relation to disability. Some read it as plain sovereignty: nothing about a human body is outside God's hand. Others stress its purpose here, that God can work through a limited speaker, and connect it with Jesus' answer about a man born blind, "so that God's works can be shown openly in him" (John 9:3), and with Paul's "my power reaches its goal in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). The verse does not say God causes every disability as a punishment.

a: send it by the hand of someone else, whoever you will send
p: An idiom for "send anyone but me." Some Jewish readers heard a reference to Aaron, or to a future redeemer.
b: The Hebrew is curt: shelach-na be-yad tishlach, "send, please, by the hand you will send." It is a polite refusal, "send someone else." Rashi says Moses meant Aaron, the one God usually sent. The Aramaic Targum Pseudo-Jonathan heard a request that God send Phinehas, whom it identifies with Elijah, the one to be sent at the end of days. Moses has run out of objections and simply does not want to go, which is why God's anger flares in the next verse.

a: The LORD's anger flared at Moses
p: God gets angry, yet gives Moses a helper. The Talmud says Moses lost the priesthood to Aaron here.
b: The anger has a strange result: not punishment but a partner. The Talmud (Zevachim 102a) records a debate. Rabbi Joshua ben Korcha says every flaring of the LORD's anger in the Torah leaves a lasting mark except this one. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says this one did too: Aaron is called "the Levite," because the priesthood, which might have been Moses', now passes to Aaron and his sons. Others note that "the Levite" is odd, since Moses is also a Levite (2:1), and suggest it means a man trained as a speaker or official. Aaron's coming "to meet you" is fulfilled in 4:27.

a: you will become as God to him
p: Moses will stand toward Aaron as God stands toward a prophet. The Aramaic Targum softens it to "master."
b: The pattern is that of prophecy: God gives words to the prophet, and the prophet speaks them. Moses will give words to Aaron, Aaron will speak them; so Moses is to Aaron "as God" (le-Elohim), and Aaron is Moses' "mouth." 7:1 says it more boldly: "I have set you as God to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother will be your prophet." Targum Onkelos, careful not to call a man God, translates "you will be to him a master" (rav). Elohim can mean God, gods, or mighty ones (as of judges in Psalm 82:6).

a: Jether
p: In one verse the Hebrew spells the name both Yeter and Yitro. Rashi had an explanation; scholars see a by-form.
b: The verse first says Yeter (Jether) and then Yitro (Jethro). Most English versions write "Jethro" both times. The forms are related (both mean "abundance, excellence"), and the ending -o may be an old name ending. Rashi, citing the Midrash, says a letter was added to his name after he added a section to the Torah, the advice of chapter 18. The difference has no effect on the meaning.

a: The men who wanted your life have all died
p: Matthew borrows these words when the angel tells Joseph to bring the child Jesus back from Egypt.
b: After Herod's death an angel tells Joseph, "The ones who wanted the child's life have died" (Matthew 2:20). The wording follows the Greek of this verse very closely, with the plural "the ones" even though only Herod is meant, just as here. Matthew tells Jesus' early life in the shape of Moses' story: a king kills babies, the child escapes, the deliverer returns once his enemies have died. Most scholars, conservative and critical, agree the echo is deliberate.

a: set them on the donkey
p: The Hebrew says "the donkey." Rashi linked it to Abraham's donkey and the Messiah's.
b: The definite article, "the donkey," caught the rabbis' attention. Rashi, drawing on Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 31, explains it as the special donkey Abraham saddled for the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22:3), on which the King Messiah will one day be revealed (Zechariah 9:9). The plain sense is just "the family donkey." The verse also speaks of Moses' "sons" though only Gershom has been named (see the variant at 2:22), and in 18:2 Moses' wife and sons are back with Jethro, so some think they returned home after 4:26.

a: But I will make his heart stubborn
t: God hardens Pharaoh's heart: the views
p: If God hardens Pharaoh's heart, is Pharaoh still to blame? Jews and Christians have answered in several ways.
b: Jewish: Rashi and Exodus Rabbah note that through the first five plagues Pharaoh hardens himself; only then does God confirm his choice. Maimonides (Laws of Repentance 6:3) teaches that a person can sin so greatly that the way of repentance is closed as a punishment. Sforno (on 7:3) answers the other way: God strengthened Pharaoh's heart so that he could still choose freely, instead of giving in only from pain. Christian: Origen (On First Principles 3.1) compared God's acts to the sun, which melts wax and hardens clay: one action, two results, depending on the material. Augustine and Calvin read it as God's just judgment, as Paul does: "he hardens the one he chooses" (Romans 9:17–18). John Chrysostom (Homilies on Romans 16) and Arminian writers such as John Wesley stress that God confirms a hardness Pharaoh chose. Critical scholars find the verbs divided among sources (see 7:3).

a: Israel is my son, my firstborn
p: God calls a whole people his firstborn son. Hosea and Matthew later build on this verse.
b: This is the first time the Bible calls Israel God's son. A firstborn held the chief place in the family and the double share of inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17). The verse sets up the logic of the last plague: Pharaoh holds God's firstborn captive, so Pharaoh's own firstborn is at stake (4:23; 11:5). Hosea recalls it, "When Israel was a boy, I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son" (Hosea 11:1), and Matthew applies those words to Jesus returning from Egypt (Matthew 2:15). Christians see Jesus as God's Son in a unique sense who sums up Israel's calling; Jewish readers stress that the sonship belongs to the people as a whole and is never revoked.

a: the LORD met him and sought to kill him
p: Right after sending Moses, the LORD tries to kill "him." Who is attacked, and why?
b: The passage (4:24–26) is short and obscure. "Him" could be Moses or his son. Jewish tradition (Talmud, Nedarim 31b–32a) says Moses had delayed his son's circumcision, and the attack was a punishment, though Rabbi Yose defends Moses: he waited because travel with a newly circumcised baby was dangerous. The Septuagint and Targum Onkelos say "an angel of the LORD" (see the variant). Christian commentators like Calvin also blamed the neglected circumcision: a leader of God's covenant people must keep its sign. Critical scholars often see an old tradition of a night attack, like Jacob's at the Jabbok (Genesis 32:24–30); William Propp suggests Moses still carried bloodguilt for killing the Egyptian.

a: a bridegroom of blood
p: Chatan damim is unexplained in the text. It may link circumcision to marriage, or blood to protection.
b: Chatan means bridegroom, or a man related by marriage; the same root gives choten, father-in-law (3:1). In Arabic the related verb khatana means "to circumcise," and Julius Wellhausen suggested circumcision was once a rite before marriage. Zipporah may be speaking to Moses ("you are my bridegroom by blood"), to the child, or to the attacker. Verse 26 says the phrase was used "about the circumcision" (la-mulot, plural). Many see a preview of the Passover: blood on the body here, blood on the doorposts in 12:13, and in both the destroyer passes by.

a: met him at God's mountain and kissed him
p: The same verb, "met," describes God's attack in 4:24 and Aaron's kiss here.
b: Pagash, "meet," connects the two scenes. On the road the LORD met Moses to kill him; at the mountain of God his brother meets him to kiss him. The reunion of two brothers at the mountain of God also recalls Jacob and Esau, who ran to meet each other and kissed (Genesis 33:4). Moses' mission now has its spokesman, as God promised (4:14).

a: The people believed
t: Belief at the start and at the end
p: Israel believes here, then loses heart (5:21; 6:9), and believes again after the sea (14:31).
b: Vayya'amen ha-'am, "the people believed," uses the verb of Genesis 15:6, where Abram "put his trust in the LORD." It fulfills God's promise to Moses (4:8–9) and forms a frame with 14:31, "they believed in the LORD and in Moses his servant." Between the two, faith will be tested hard: the bricks-without-straw crisis (5:21), the deaf ears of 6:9, and the terror at the sea (14:11–12). The rhythm of belief, collapse and renewed belief marks Israel's whole wilderness story.

a: let them keep a feast for me
p: Chag is a festival people travel to keep, a pilgrimage. The Arabic hajj comes from the same root.
b: Ve-yachoggu li, "let them hold a chag to me." A chag is a feast kept by going to a holy place, often with dancing in procession; the same root gives the Arabic hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca. Israel's three great pilgrim feasts (23:14–17) are each a chag. The first request is not for political freedom but for freedom to worship, which in the ancient world was never separate from the question of who is your master.

a: Who is this LORD, that I should heed his voice
p: Pharaoh's question sets the agenda for the plagues: by the end, Egypt will "know that I am the LORD."
b: Pharaoh, regarded in Egypt as a god and son of the sun-god Ra, sees no reason to listen to the god of a slave people. His words "I do not know the LORD" are answered again and again: "Here is how you will know that I am the LORD" (7:17), "so that you know that none is like the LORD our God" (8:10), "Egypt will know that I am the LORD" (14:4, 18). Jewish and Christian readers alike see the plagues as a contest of knowledge, a long answer to this question.

a: The God of the Hebrews
p: Egyptian and Canaanite texts speak of Habiru or 'Apiru, uprooted outsiders. Were they the Hebrews?
b: In the Bible, "Hebrew" is mostly what outsiders call Israelites, or what Israelites call themselves before foreigners (1:15; 2:6; Genesis 39:14; Jonah 1:9). Texts from across the Near East in the second millennium BC mention Habiru or 'Apiru, people outside the normal social order: hired soldiers, laborers, raiders. The Amarna letters of the 1300s BC complain of them in Canaan, and Egyptian texts record them as workers. Most scholars think the words are related and that some early Israelites may have been counted among such people, but that the groups were not identical: 'Apiru was a social label found from Mesopotamia to Egypt, not one nation.

a: you would give them a rest
p: The verb is hishbatt, from shavat, the root of "Sabbath." A midrash says Moses won Israel a weekly rest.
b: Ve-hishbattem, "you would make them stop," comes from shavat, "cease, rest," the root of Shabbat. For Pharaoh, rest is idleness (5:8, 17). Exodus Rabbah (1:28) tells that Moses, growing up in the palace, persuaded Pharaoh that slaves would work better with one day of rest in seven, and chose the seventh day. The story is legend, but it captures a real link: Deuteronomy 5:15 grounds the Sabbath in the memory of slavery in Egypt.

a: the drivers over the people and to its officers
p: Egyptian drivers stand over Israelite foremen who answer for each day's bricks. Egyptian records show such quotas.
b: The nogesim are Pharaoh's drivers; the shoterim, probably "record keepers" (compare Akkadian shataru, "to write"), are Israelites who must answer for their crews (5:14). Egyptian records show similar systems. A leather scroll in the Louvre from year 5 of Ramesses II lists brickmaking crews with their quotas and shortfalls, and texts from the workmen's village at Deir el-Medina record days missed and reasons given. Kitchen and Hoffmeier cite such documents as background that fits the story. Later the shoterim become officials in Israel itself (Numbers 11:16; Deuteronomy 16:18).

a: Let the labor weigh heavy on the men
p: Pharaoh makes the labor "heavy" (kaved), the same word soon used for his heart.
b: Tikhbad ha-'avodah, "let the labor be heavy." Kaved, heavy, is a key word in Exodus. Moses is heavy of mouth (4:10); Pharaoh's heart is heavy (7:14; 8:15; 9:7); the plagues are heavy (8:24; 9:3, 18; 10:14); and the LORD will "win glory," ikkavedah, literally "make myself heavy," over Pharaoh (14:4). Kavod, "glory," is God's weightiness, which fills the tabernacle at the end of the book (40:34). Pharaoh's attempt to crush Israel with weight is answered by the weight of God.

a: the wrong is your own people's
p: The Hebrew is awkward: literally "your people sin." The Greek reads "you wrong your people."
b: Ve-chatat 'ammekha is grammatically unusual, literally "and your people sins" or "and the sin is your people." The foremen seem to mean that Pharaoh's own Egyptians, the drivers, are at fault, not the Israelite workers. The Septuagint read it as "you will wrong your people," taking Israel as Pharaoh's people. The foremen still call themselves "your servants" three times; they appeal to Pharaoh as a fair master, and do not yet look to the LORD.

a: You have made us reek
p: A vivid Hebrew idiom for being hated. Jacob says the same to Simeon and Levi in Genesis 34:30.
b: Hiv'ashtem et-rechenu, literally "you have made our smell stink." It means "you have made us odious." Jacob uses it after Simeon and Levi's massacre at Shechem: "You have made me stink among the people of the land" (Genesis 34:30), and Saul's army uses it of Israel before the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:4). The same verb describes the Nile after it turns to blood (7:18, 21), so the stench the foremen fear will soon be Egypt's own.

a: why have you brought harm on this people?
p: Moses accuses God of doing harm. Jewish tradition both admires and rebukes his boldness.
b: Moses' words are sharp: "why have you done harm (hare'otah)?" and "you have not rescued." This is the language of lament, found in many psalms (Psalm 44:23–24; 88:14) and in Habakkuk 1:2–4, where faith argues with God instead of falling silent. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 111a) imagines God answering with a sigh for the patriarchs, who were promised a land and never questioned him. Other readers see Moses as a model of honest prayer, and note that God answers not with a rebuke but with a promise (6:1).

a: Forced by a strong hand
p: The "strong hand" is God's, forcing Pharaoh. Some read it as Pharaoh's own hand, driving Israel out in haste.
b: Ki ve-yad chazaqah yeshallechem can mean "because of a strong hand he will send them": the LORD's hand will force him (3:19–20). Rashi reads the second half as Pharaoh's own forceful hand: he will drive them out in a hurry, even against their will, as happens in 12:33. Both meanings come true. The verse is God's answer to Moses' complaint in 5:22–23: not an explanation, but a promise, "Now you will see."

a: God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am the LORD.
p: 6:2–8 retells the call of chapter 3 in a new style. Is it a renewal, or another source?
b: In 6:2–13 God again tells Moses his name, recalls the fathers, promises the land and sends him to Pharaoh, and Moses again objects about his speech, now in Egypt rather than at the bush. Traditional readers see a renewal of the call after the failure of chapter 5: God goes back to the foundations. Source critics assign 6:2–12 to the Priestly writer (P), whose account of Moses' call parallels the older account in chapters 3–4 (J and E). Many scholars of both kinds note that the final form works as a story: the name given in chapter 3 is now explained by what God is about to do.

a: I appeared as God Almighty
p: "God Almighty" translates El Shaddai, the name God uses with Abraham and Jacob. Its root meaning is uncertain.
b: In Genesis God says "I am God Almighty" to Abram (Genesis 17:1) and to Jacob (Genesis 35:11), and Jacob blesses Joseph "by the Almighty" with "blessings of breasts and womb" (Genesis 49:25). "Almighty" comes from the Greek pantokratōr and Latin omnipotens. The original sense is debated: "God of the mountain" (Akkadian shadû, mountain), "God of the breast," or from shadad, "destroy, overpower." The Talmud (Chagigah 12a) explains Shaddai as she-dai, "who said 'Enough!'" to his creation. The name is tied to promises of offspring.
r: Genesis 17:1; Genesis 28:3; Genesis 35:11; Genesis 48:3; Genesis 49:25; Ruth 1:20

a: But my name, the LORD, I did not make known to them.
p: In Genesis the fathers use the name LORD often. So what does "I did not make known" mean?
b: God says "I am the LORD" to Abram (Genesis 15:7) and Jacob (Genesis 28:13). Source critics since Jean Astruc (1753) take 6:3 as a key clue: the Priestly writer held that the name was first revealed to Moses, while the Yahwist used it from creation on. Jewish commentators answer that the fathers knew the name but not what it stood for: Rashi says they did not know God "by my attribute of faithfulness," keeping his promises, which Israel is about to see; Ramban and Cassuto similarly. Some read it as a question: "did I not make myself known?" R. W. L. Moberly argues that Genesis tells the fathers' story using the name in the light of Moses' later faith.
orig: וּשְׁמִי יְהוָה לֹא נוֹדַעְתִּי לָהֶם (u-shemi YHWH lo noda'ti lahem)

a: I will redeem you with my arm stretched out
p: Ga'al is the word for a relative who buys back a family member from slavery. God claims that role for Israel.
b: Ve-ga'alti, "I will redeem." A go'el was the near relative bound to rescue family members: to buy back land or a kinsman sold into slavery (Leviticus 25:25, 47–49), to avenge blood, or to marry a widow, as Boaz did for Ruth (Ruth 3:9–13). Here God acts as Israel's next of kin. "Outstretched arm" may answer Egyptian royal language: Pharaohs were praised as "strong of arm," and James Hoffmeier has argued that Exodus deliberately sets the arm of the LORD against the arm of Pharaoh. Deuteronomy repeats the phrase as a creed (Deuteronomy 26:8).
r: 15:13; Leviticus 25:47–49; Deuteronomy 26:8; Ruth 3:9–13; Isaiah 43:1; Isaiah 51:9–10; Luke 24:21; Acts 13:17

a: I will take you to myself as a people
p: The four verbs of promise in 6:6–7 became the four cups of wine drunk at the Passover Seder.
b: Jewish tradition counts four expressions of redemption here: "I will lead you out," "I will snatch you," "I will redeem you," "I will take you." Among several explanations for the four cups of wine required at the Seder, the Jerusalem Talmud (Pesachim 10:1) connects them with these four verbs. The next verb, "I will bring you" (6:8), led to debate over a fifth cup; custom resolved it with a cup poured but not drunk, the "cup of Elijah," waiting for the prophet who will announce the final redemption. Christian scholars note that one of these cups, "the cup after supper," is likely the cup Jesus blessed (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25).

a: and I will be God to you
p: "You will be my people and I will be your God" sums up the covenant from Exodus to Revelation.
b: This pairing is often called the covenant formula. It appears in the Torah (Leviticus 26:12; Deuteronomy 29:13), in the new covenant promise (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:28), in Paul (2 Corinthians 6:16), and at the end of the Bible: "They will be his peoples, and God himself will be with them and be their God" (Revelation 21:3). In Exodus it is spoken before the covenant is made at Sinai, as the goal toward which the rescue moves.

a: I lifted my hand in oath
p: "I lifted my hand" means "I swore." People swore by raising a hand toward heaven.
b: Nasa'ti et-yadi, "I raised my hand," is the gesture of oath-taking. Abram tells the king of Sodom he has raised his hand to the LORD (Genesis 14:22), and God says in Deuteronomy 32:40, "I lift my hand to the sky / and swear, As I live forever." God swearing an oath is a way of speaking about the unbreakable certainty of his promise (Hebrews 6:13–18).

a: their spirit was worn short
p: Qotser ruach can mean short breath, impatience, or a spirit crushed by suffering.
b: Mi-qotser ruach, "from shortness of spirit (or breath)." Ruach means breath, wind and spirit. The phrase can mean impatience (Micah 2:7; Job 21:4) or exhaustion: people panting under hard work have no breath left to hope. Rashi explains it as the short, rapid breathing of someone in distress. The people who "believed" in 4:31 now cannot even listen; the beating of chapter 5 has taken their breath away.

a: and I with uncircumcised lips
p: An image of lips that are closed or blocked, unfit for God's use. Ears and hearts can be "uncircumcised" too.
b: 'Aral sefatayim, "uncircumcised of lips." The Bible uses "uncircumcised" for any organ that is covered or closed and so cannot do its work: uncircumcised ears that cannot hear (Jeremiah 6:10), uncircumcised hearts that will not obey (Leviticus 26:41; Deuteronomy 10:16), fruit trees whose first fruit is forbidden (Leviticus 19:23). Moses means he cannot speak well, much like "heavy of mouth" (4:10). After the circumcision scene of 4:24–26, the image carries extra force.

a: These are the heads of their fathers' houses.
p: The story stops for a genealogy, then picks up where it left off. The list exists to place Moses and Aaron.
b: The list begins with Reuben and Simeon as if it would cover all twelve tribes, but stops at Levi and runs down to Aaron's grandson Phinehas. Its point is to set the two leaders in their family before the contest with Pharaoh begins, and to show Aaron's priestly line. 6:28–30 repeat 6:10–12, a device scholars call "resumptive repetition," which signals that the story is resuming after an insertion. Source critics assign the list to P. Rashi suggests Reuben and Simeon are mentioned because, like Levi, they were rebuked by Jacob (Genesis 49:3–7), and the list honors them anyway.

a: The years of Amram's life were one hundred and thirty-seven
p: Levi, Kohath, Amram, Moses: four generations. Their ages cannot fill 430 years in Egypt unless the list skips names.
b: Kohath came down to Egypt with Jacob (Genesis 46:11). If Kohath lived 133 years and Amram 137, and Moses was 80 at the exodus (7:7), the longest possible time from the descent to the exodus is about 350 years, and much less if the generations overlap. Yet 12:40 says Israel lived in Egypt 430 years. One answer: the genealogy names only key ancestors and skips generations, as many ancient lists do (Kitchen); compare 1 Chronicles 7:22–27, which counts about ten generations from Ephraim to Joshua. Another: the 430 years include the patriarchs' time in Canaan, as the Samaritan Pentateuch and Septuagint read 12:40, leaving about 215 years in Egypt. Genesis 15:16 also says "the fourth generation" will return. The Septuagint reads "in the fifth generation" in 13:18 (see there), and its manuscripts are reported to give somewhat different life spans for Kohath and Amram, a point this edition has not been able to verify.

a: Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon
p: Aaron marries into Judah's leading family. Nahshon is an ancestor of David, and Elisheba's name becomes Elizabeth.
b: Nahshon son of Amminadab is the leader of Judah in the wilderness (Numbers 1:7; 2:3) and an ancestor of Boaz and David (Ruth 4:19–22; Matthew 1:4). So the priestly line of Aaron is joined by marriage to the future royal line. Elisheba, "my God is an oath (or abundance)," is the Hebrew form of Elizabeth: in Luke 1:5, John the Baptist's mother Elizabeth is "of the daughters of Aaron," a deliberate echo.
r: Numbers 1:7; Numbers 2:3; Ruth 4:19–22; 1 Chronicles 2:10; Matthew 1:4; Luke 1:5

a: Putiel
p: Several names in Moses' family look Egyptian: Moses, Phinehas, perhaps Putiel and Merari.
b: Phinehas matches the Egyptian name Pa-nehasy, "the Nubian," well attested in New Kingdom Egypt. Putiel may combine Egyptian p3-di, "the one given by," with Hebrew El, "God" (compare Potiphar, Genesis 39:1). Moses is probably Egyptian (see 2:10), and some link Merari and Hophni (1 Samuel 1:3) with Egyptian words too. Hoffmeier and others argue that these names, found especially among Levites, preserve a real memory of a stay in Egypt. Critical scholars such as Friedman use the same evidence to argue that the Levites, in particular, came out of Egypt.

a: in their ranks like armies
p: Tsava means army or host. Israel leaves Egypt organized like the LORD's army, not as a mob of runaways.
b: 'Al-tsiv'otam, "by their armies (hosts)." The word appears again at the exodus itself: "all the armies of the LORD went out" (12:41, 51), and the people go up "in battle order" (13:18). The same noun gives God's title YHWH Tseva'ot, "the LORD of hosts" or "of armies." The slaves are being described in military terms, as a nation marching out under its commander.

a: Aaron your brother will be your prophet
p: This verse is the Bible's clearest definition of a prophet: one who speaks for another.
b: God puts it plainly: Moses will be "as God" to Pharaoh, and Aaron will be his navi, his prophet. A prophet is not first a fortune teller but a spokesman, the mouth through which another's words come (4:15–16). The same pattern defines Israel's prophets: "I will put my words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him" (Deuteronomy 18:18). Moses himself is later counted the greatest prophet (Deuteronomy 34:10).

a: I will make Pharaoh's heart hard
t: Three words for a hard heart
p: Exodus uses three verbs: "make strong (stubborn)," "make heavy" and "make hard." This translation keeps them apart.
b: About twenty times the story speaks of Pharaoh's heart. Chazaq, "strong, firm," here translated "stubborn," is the most common (4:21; 7:13; 9:12; 14:4). Kaved, "heavy" (7:14; 8:15; 9:34; 10:1), may echo the Egyptian belief that at death the heart was weighed against the feather of Ma'at, truth: a heavy heart meant condemnation (Book of the Dead, spell 125). Qashah, "hard" (7:3; 13:15), is used least. God is the subject ten times (4:21; 7:3; 9:12; 10:1, 20, 27; 11:10; 14:4, 8, 17) and Pharaoh three (8:15, 32; 9:34), plus the retelling in 13:15; the rest are neutral ("was stubborn"). Ramban (on 7:3) gives two answers: the hardening was a just penalty for Pharaoh's earlier cruelty, and it let him keep refusing from his own will rather than yield only to pain. Robert Wilson suggested that chazaq belongs to the Priestly source and kaved to the older Yahwist. Most English versions say "harden" for all three, which hides the variety.

a: by great judgments
p: The plagues fall into three groups of three, with a pattern of warnings, before the final blow.
b: Exodus calls the plagues "signs," "wonders," "judgments" and "blows" (makkot, negef). Readers since the Middle Ages, and scholars such as Moshe Greenberg and Nahum Sarna, note a pattern. Plagues 1, 4 and 7 begin with Moses meeting Pharaoh in the morning by the water (7:15; 8:20; 9:13); plagues 2, 5 and 8 begin with "go in to Pharaoh" (8:1; 9:1; 10:1); plagues 3, 6 and 9 come with no warning at all (8:16; 9:8; 10:21). The tenth stands alone. The Passover Haggadah preserves Rabbi Judah's memory aid for the ten, a three-part acronym, D'tzach Adash B'achav. Source critics find J, E and P plague accounts woven together, which explains why Aaron's staff appears in some and not others.

a: Moses was eighty years old
p: Stephen divides Moses' 120 years into three forties: in Egypt, in Midian, and in the wilderness.
b: Deuteronomy 34:7 says Moses died at 120. Stephen's speech fills in the pattern: forty years in Egypt (Acts 7:23), forty in Midian before the bush (Acts 7:30), and forty leading Israel in the wilderness (Acts 7:36). Rabbinic tradition (Sifre on Deuteronomy) notes the same three periods. Aaron, at eighty-three, is the older brother. Exodus gives the ages here, as a formal record, because the mission now begins.

a: It will become a serpent
p: This is tannin, not the nachash of 4:3. Tannin can mean a great serpent, a crocodile, or the sea monster.
b: In 4:3 the staff became a nachash, an ordinary snake. Here it becomes a tannin, the word for the great sea creatures of Genesis 1:21 and for the chaos monster God defeats (Psalm 74:13; Isaiah 27:1; 51:9). Ezekiel calls Pharaoh himself "the great tannin sprawled among his river channels" (Ezekiel 29:3), probably the crocodile, a sacred animal in Egypt. So when Aaron's tannin swallows the magicians' staffs, the image is of Egypt's own power symbol being swallowed. 7:15 calls it a nachash again, so the words overlap.
r: 4:3; 7:15; Genesis 1:21; Psalm 74:13; Isaiah 27:1; Isaiah 51:9–10; Ezekiel 29:3; Revelation 12:9

a: the magicians of Egypt
p: Chartummim are Egyptian priest-scholars. Later tradition named two of them Jannes and Jambres.
b: Chartummim comes from the Egyptian title hry-tp, "chief lector priest," a learned priest who read sacred spells; the word also appears in the Joseph story (Genesis 41:8) and in Daniel. Egyptian stories, such as the tales in Papyrus Westcar, tell of such priests making wax crocodiles come alive. Jewish tradition named two of Moses' opponents: the Damascus Document from Qumran calls them Yohanah and his brother, Targum Pseudo-Jonathan names Jannes and Jambres, and Paul uses those names in 2 Timothy 3:8. Some modern writers suggest the snakes were cobras made rigid by pressure on the neck, a trick of snake charmers. The text simply reports that they matched the sign, and were beaten.

a: Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs
p: Aaron's staff swallows the magicians' staffs. At the sea, "the earth swallowed them" (15:12).
b: Vayyivla', "swallowed," is the first hint of the outcome. The same verb returns in the Song of the Sea: "You stretched out your right hand. The earth swallowed them" (15:12). The magicians can copy the sign, but they cannot keep what they made. The Talmud and the Midrash note that it was the staff, not the serpent, that swallowed: the miracle within the miracle.

a: Look, he is going out to the water
p: Why is Pharaoh at the Nile at dawn? For ritual, for inspection, or, says the Midrash, to hide a human need.
b: Pharaoh may have gone out to inspect the Nile's rising, on which all Egypt's harvest depended, or for a morning rite to the Nile god Hapi. The Midrash (Exodus Rabbah 9:8), quoted by Rashi, has a sharper answer: Pharaoh claimed to be a god who had no bodily needs, so he went down to the river early each morning, where no one would see him, to relieve himself. Moses is to meet him exactly there. The joke makes a serious point: the man who claims to be divine is only human.

a: it will be turned to blood
p: Some find natural causes behind the plagues, beginning with a red, poisoned Nile. Others see pure miracle.
b: In 1957 Greta Hort proposed a chain of events: an extreme summer flood carrying red earth and toxic algae turns the Nile "blood" red and kills the fish; frogs flee the river and die; insects breed in the rotting frogs; disease, perhaps anthrax, kills cattle and causes sores; then hail, locusts and a desert sandstorm (darkness) follow. Colin Humphreys and others have refined such theories, and Siro Trevisanato linked the plagues to ash and acid rain from the Thera (Santorini) eruption, though that eruption is usually dated about 1600 BC, long before either exodus date. Supporters, including many believers, say God used nature, and the miracle lies in the timing, the warnings, the intensity and the sparing of Goshen. Others answer that the text presents real blood (2 Kings 3:22 shows "like blood" was available) and wonders beyond nature. Critical scholars think the list grew in the telling, from shorter earlier versions (compare Psalm 78; 105).

a: Egypt will find it cannot bear to drink water from the Nile
p: The Samaritan Pentateuch and a Dead Sea Scroll repeat each command as a report that Moses carried it out.
b: In the plague stories the standard Hebrew often gives God's command to Moses but not the scene in which Moses says it to Pharaoh. The Samaritan Pentateuch, and before it the Qumran scroll 4QpaleoExod-m (about 100–25 BC), fill these gaps: after this verse they add a paragraph in which Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh and repeat the words of 7:16–18 (see the variant on this verse). Similar additions follow other commands, after 8:1, 8:20, 9:1, 9:13 and 10:3, and before 11:4. Judith Sanderson showed that the scroll shares these expansions with the Samaritan tradition, so they were not a sectarian invention but part of a widely used Jewish text type. They add no new content, so the Plain English follows the shorter Hebrew.

a: even in wood and in stone
p: Most read this as water stored in wooden and stone jars. Some think of trees and rocks, or even idols.
b: The Hebrew says only uva-'etsim uva-'avanim, "and in the woods and in the stones." The usual reading supplies "vessels": even the water already drawn into jars was affected. Others take "wood and stone" as sap in trees and water in rock pools. A third reading, found in the Midrash, notes that since "wood and stone" is a common biblical phrase for idols (Deuteronomy 4:28), so the images of Egypt's gods, washed daily by priests, were stained with blood. The plain sense is that no water in Egypt escaped.

a: all the water in the Nile was turned to blood
p: An Egyptian poem says "the river is blood." Some call it a record of the exodus. Most scholars disagree.
b: The Admonitions of Ipuwer, preserved in a papyrus of about 1250 BC (Papyrus Leiden I 344) but probably composed centuries earlier, laments a time of chaos in Egypt: "the river is blood," servants rule, the poor become rich, "gold is around the necks of slave women." Immanuel Velikovsky and later David Rohl linked it with the exodus. Most Egyptologists, including Miriam Lichtheim, read it as a literary lament about social disorder, a known genre, not an eyewitness report; its date and themes do not match. The verdict: a striking parallel of image, not a historical record of the plagues.

a: But the magicians of Egypt did the same with their spells
p: The magicians can only add more blood. They cannot undo the plague.
b: If all the water in Egypt was blood, where did the magicians find water to change? Rashi says they used water from Goshen, where Israel lived; others point to the wells dug in 7:24. The story's point is ironic: Egypt's experts can match the sign, but only by making their own people's suffering worse. They never once reverse a plague. By the third plague they fail (8:18), and by the sixth they cannot even stand before Moses (9:11).

a: Go in to Pharaoh
p: In Hebrew Bibles, 8:1–4 here is the end of chapter 7 (7:26–29), so chapter 8 is numbered four verses behind.
b: The chapter breaks were added in the Middle Ages, and Christian and Jewish printings put this one in different places. In the Hebrew Bible the frog warning closes chapter 7 (7:26–29), and Hebrew 8:1 is English 8:5. Throughout chapter 8, then, the Hebrew verse number is four less than the English (English 8:32 = Hebrew 8:28). This translation follows the English numbering, which most English readers and tools use.
