a: The Nile will swarm with frogs
p: Egypt honored Heqet, a goddess with a frog's head who helped at childbirth. Here frogs become a curse.
b: Frogs were a sign of life and fertility in Egypt, because they appeared in great numbers as the Nile's flood went down. The goddess Heqet, shown with a frog's head, was linked with birth and was said to shape children. Many interpreters, such as John Currid, see the plague as a mockery of what Egypt held sacred: the symbol of new life fills ovens and beds and then rots in heaps. The verb "swarm" (sharats) is the creation word of Genesis 1:20, where the waters "swarm with swarming things that live"; here creation runs wild against Egypt.

a: Up came the frogs
p: The Hebrew word is singular: "the frog came up." A Midrash pictures one giant frog that kept multiplying.
b: Hebrew says vatta'al ha-tsefarde'a, "and the frog came up." In ordinary Hebrew this is a collective, like "the fish" in English, and 8:5 and 8:7 use the plural. But in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 67b) Rabbi Akiva says there was one frog and it filled the land of Egypt; Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah answers that one frog whistled and the rest came. Rashi quotes a midrash in which the frog bred new swarms each time it was struck, then gives the plain sense, a swarm. It is a good example of rabbinic play with grammar.

a: none is like the LORD our God
p: A theme of the plagues: Pharaoh must learn that the LORD has no equal. It peaks in the Song of the Sea.
b: The plagues are presented as a lesson in knowing: "you will know that I am the LORD" (7:17), "none is like the LORD" (8:10), "none like me in all the earth" (9:14), "the earth is the LORD's own" (9:29). Pharaoh's first words were "Who is this LORD...? I do not know the LORD" (5:2). The answer comes in the Song of the Sea: "Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?" (15:11). Even the timing Pharaoh chooses, "tomorrow," lets him see that the frogs leave by Moses' word and not by chance.

a: piles and piles
t: Heaps of frogs, heaps of clay
p: "Heaps" is chomarim, the same root as chomer, the clay Israel had to work into bricks.
b: The Hebrew doubles the word, chomarim chomarim, "heaps heaps," to stress the huge number. The root chmr also gave chomer, the "clay" or "mortar" of Israel's bitter slavery (1:14). Many readers see a deliberate echo: Egypt made Israel pile up clay, and now Egypt piles up the rotting dead frogs, and "the land stank." Compare 5:21, where Israel's foremen say Moses has made them "reek" before Pharaoh: now it is Egypt that reeks.

a: gnats
p: The insect called kinnim is uncertain: gnats, lice (KJV), mosquitoes or sand flies.
b: Kinnim (here kinnam) appears almost only in this story. The Talmud, Rashi and the KJV understood lice, which fits creatures "on people and on animals." The Septuagint says skniphes, small biting insects, and Philo and Origen describe them as gnats or mosquitoes. Modern lexicons lean toward gnats or mosquitoes, which would breed in the standing water after the Nile's flood. Coming from "the dust of the ground," the plague also echoes God's promise that Abraham's offspring would be like the dust (Genesis 13:16).

a: It is the finger of God
p: The magicians admit defeat. Jesus later uses the same phrase of his own power over demons.
b: When Egypt's experts cannot match the gnats, they say etsba' Elohim hi, "it is the finger of God." They use "God" in general, not the name of Israel's LORD, perhaps admitting only that some divine power is at work, perhaps hinting that their own gods were outdone. The phrase returns in the tablets "written by God's own finger" (31:18). Jesus says, "If it is by God's finger that I throw out demons, then God's kingdom has already reached you" (Luke 11:20). The Passover Haggadah reasons from "finger" here and "hand" in 14:31 that Egypt suffered ten blows in Egypt and fifty at the sea, five times as many.

a: the swarm
p: 'Arov means "mixture." Rashi says wild beasts; the Greek says dog-flies.
b: The Hebrew he-'arov is from a root meaning "mix." Rashi, following the Midrash, explains it as a mixed horde of wild animals, snakes and scorpions. The Septuagint reads kynomyia, the "dog-fly," a biting fly; Psalm 78:45 says the swarm "devoured" them. Most modern scholars take it as flies, perhaps the stable fly, which carries disease and could explain the cattle plague and sores that follow, as Greta Hort argued. The Plain English keeps the general word "swarm."

a: I will set apart the land of Goshen
p: From now on, Israel's region is spared. Goshen lay in the eastern Nile Delta.
b: Goshen, where Jacob's family settled (Genesis 45:10; 47:27), was in the eastern Nile Delta, probably the Wadi Tumilat region near modern Tell el-Maskhuta, good land for herds. In plagues one to three, the text does not say Israel was spared; from the fourth on, it does, and the distinction becomes the point: "you will know that I am the LORD, here in the middle of the land." The LORD is not only the God of a far mountain; he acts inside Egypt.

a: a thing the Egyptians abhor
p: Moses says Israel's sacrifices would disgust the Egyptians. Possibly the animals were sacred, or the rites foreign.
b: To'evah, "an abhorrent thing," also describes Egypt's attitude toward eating with Hebrews (Genesis 43:32) and toward shepherds (Genesis 46:34). Ancient and medieval interpreters (Onkelos, Rashi, Ibn Ezra) explain that the sheep, goats and cattle Israel would offer were sacred animals in Egypt, such as the ram of Amun or the Apis bull; Onkelos even translates "we would sacrifice the animals the Egyptians worship." Others think the offense lay in the rites themselves, which were not Egyptian. The point stands either way: worship of the LORD cannot be done on Egypt's terms.

a: on the camels
p: Domesticated camels were rare in Egypt and Canaan before about 1000 BC. Is the mention an anachronism?
b: Camels appear in Genesis and here among Egypt's herds. Excavations in the Aravah valley led Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef (2013) to date the first large use of domestic camels in the southern Levant to the late 900s BC, and camels are scarcely shown in Egyptian art before the first millennium. Critical scholars take the camels as a detail from the writers' own later time. Defenders such as Kenneth Kitchen point to scattered earlier evidence (bones, figurines, a camel-hair rope) and argue that a few camels could be known long before they were common. The list may simply name every kind of beast a reader would picture.

a: All Egypt's livestock died
p: If all Egypt's livestock died, how could hail kill livestock later (9:19–25)?
b: Several answers are given. (1) The plague struck only animals "out in the field" (9:3), so those in stalls survived; this is Ramban's and Ibn Ezra's view. (2) "All" in Hebrew often means "a great many," as in "the whole world came to Egypt" (Genesis 41:57). (3) Egypt could have bought or taken animals afterward. (4) Source critics see different plague accounts stitched together, each complete in itself. The story's point is the contrast: "not one" of Israel's animals died, a fact Pharaoh checks for himself (9:7).

a: soot from a kiln
p: Moses throws furnace ash into the air. Some see the brick kilns of Israel's slavery turned against Egypt.
b: The kivshan is a kiln or furnace, the word used for the smoke rising from Sodom (Genesis 19:28) and from Sinai (19:18). Brick kilns were where Israel suffered; Deuteronomy calls Egypt "the iron furnace" (Deuteronomy 4:20). Nahum Sarna and others note the irony: the ash of slavery becomes the dust of judgment. Some have also linked the act with Egyptian rites in which ashes were scattered to bless the land; here they curse it.

a: sores that burst open in blisters
p: Shechin is an inflamed sore. Deuteronomy later threatens Israel with "the boils of Egypt."
b: Shechin is an inflamed swelling; it is the illness of Job (Job 2:7) and of King Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:7). Here the sores "break out" into ava'bu'ot, blisters. Suggested diagnoses include skin anthrax (spread from the dead cattle of plague five, Hort), smallpox, or an insect-borne infection. Deuteronomy warns that if Israel breaks the covenant, the LORD will strike them "with the boils of Egypt" (28:27, 35): the plagues become a warning for Israel too.
r: Leviticus 13:18–20; Deuteronomy 28:27; Deuteronomy 28:35; Job 2:7; 2 Kings 20:7; Revelation 16:2

a: But the LORD made Pharaoh's heart stubborn
p: In the first five plagues Pharaoh hardens himself. Only now, at the sixth, does God harden him. Why?
b: God foretold it (4:21; 7:3), but this is the first time the narrator says God did it. Jewish tradition reads the order as key: Pharaoh freely hardened himself five times, so God then removed his chance to repent as punishment (Exodus Rabbah 13; Rashi on 7:3; Maimonides, Laws of Repentance 6:3). Origen said the same sun that melts wax hardens clay: God's acts reveal what a heart already is. Calvin and later Reformed writers read it as God's sovereign choice, as Paul does in Romans 9:17–18. Sforno (on 7:3) argued that "made strong" means God gave Pharaoh the strength to keep choosing freely, so that any release would be real repentance and not mere escape from pain; Ramban gives this view alongside the penalty view.

a: all my blows into your heart
p: The Hebrew says God will send all his blows "to your heart." The final plagues target Pharaoh himself.
b: El-libbekha, "to your heart," is unusual. Many versions smooth it to "on you" or "on you yourself." Rashi takes it as a hint that the death of the firstborn would weigh as much as all the other blows together, the blow that would strike Pharaoh's heart, his own son. Others read it as the inner target of the plagues: the heart that has grown heavy and stubborn. The Plain keeps the odd phrase because "heart" is the key word of the whole story.

a: for this reason I have kept you standing
p: Paul quotes this verse in Romans 9:17, but says "I raised you up," a step beyond "kept you standing."
b: The Hebrew he'emadtikha means "I caused you to stand," that is, kept you alive instead of wiping you out (9:15). The Septuagint says "you were kept safe." Paul writes, "I raised you up for just this" (Romans 9:17), which can sound like God brought Pharaoh to power. Paul draws the conclusion: "he shows mercy to the one he chooses, and he hardens the one he chooses" (Romans 9:18). Interpreters divide over whether Paul speaks of individual destiny (Augustine, Calvin) or of God's purpose in history to spread his name. Arminians read the passage as conditional election, God hardening those who first resist (Jacobus Arminius on Romans 9; John Wesley), and some, like Brian Abasciano, read it as corporate election of a people; John Chrysostom stressed Pharaoh's own choice.

a: Those of Pharaoh's servants who feared the word of the LORD
p: For the first time, some Egyptians take the LORD seriously. Some may have joined the "mixed crowd" of 12:38.
b: The hail is the first plague that comes with advice on how to escape it, and some of Pharaoh's own officials heed it. One rabbinic tradition, which made Job one of Pharaoh's advisers (Talmud, Sotah 11a), finds him among those who "feared" (compare Job 1:1), and contrasts them with those who "did not set their heart" on God's word. The verse shows that the plagues are not aimed at Egyptians merely as Egyptians: whoever listens is spared. Many link them with the "mixed crowd" that left Egypt with Israel (12:38).

a: the LORD sent thunder
p: The Hebrew for thunder is qolot, "voices": the same word used for the thunder at Sinai.
b: Hebrew has no separate word for thunder; it says qolot, "voices" or "sounds." Pharaoh begs for an end to "God's voices" (9:28). The same word fills the scene at Sinai: "there were thunders and lightning" (19:16; 20:18). Psalm 29 speaks of "the voice of the LORD" seven times in a storm. The Plain uses "thunder," but the reader should hear God speaking in it.

a: The LORD is the righteous one
p: Pharaoh confesses sin in legal language. Was it real repentance?
b: Pharaoh speaks like the guilty party in a lawsuit: the LORD is ha-tsaddiq, "the one in the right," and he and his people are ha-resha'im, "the ones in the wrong." Moses doubts it (9:30), and Pharaoh's change lasts only until the hail stops (9:34). Some Jewish commentators (Exodus Rabbah; Rashbam) see a real moment of fear. Christian writers often used the passage to separate regret driven by fear of punishment from true turning to God (compare 2 Corinthians 7:10).

a: the earth is the LORD's own
p: Moses' words become the opening line of Psalm 24 and are quoted by Paul.
b: "The earth is the LORD's own" (la-YHWH ha-arets) is the claim behind all the plagues: the LORD is not a local god of Israel's tribes but the owner of Egypt's land too. Psalm 24:1 begins with the same words, and Paul quotes the psalm when he tells Christians that food sold in markets belongs to God (1 Corinthians 10:26). Exodus 19:5 makes the same claim: "the whole earth belongs to me."

a: the barley had formed its ears and the flax was budding
p: Barley ripens and flax blooms in Egypt around February–March, setting the hail a few weeks before Passover.
b: In Egypt, flax flowers and barley heads out in about January to February, while wheat and spelt (emmer) ripen a month or so later. This detail fits the land well and puts the hail roughly six to eight weeks before the spring Passover. The barley is aviv, "in the ear," the same word that names the month of the exodus (13:4). Scholars such as Kitchen and Hoffmeier cite these farming details as signs of real knowledge of Egypt; others reply that anyone in the region knew such seasons.

a: so that you can tell in the ears of your son and your son's son
p: The plagues are told so that parents will retell them. This verse is a root of the Passover Seder.
b: Exodus repeatedly turns events into lessons for the next generation (12:26–27; 13:8; 13:14). The Passover Haggadah is built on this command: "In every generation a person must see himself as if he came out of Egypt." The verb hit'allalti, here "I made sport of," means to deal harshly or mockingly with someone; the Philistine priests use it when they recall how God "dealt harshly" with Egypt (1 Samuel 6:6), and it describes Saul's fear that his enemies would "make sport" of him (1 Samuel 31:4). God's acts are told as a humbling of the proud.

a: Until when will you refuse to bend low before me?
p: "Bend low" is the verb used of Egypt afflicting Israel. Now Pharaoh must be afflicted.
b: The verb 'anah, "to be bowed down, humbled," is the same root used for Egypt's "afflicting" Israel in 1:11–12 and in God's promise to Abraham that his offspring would be "afflicted" four hundred years (Genesis 15:13). The tables are turning. In the Haggadah, the bread of Passover is called lechem 'oni, "bread of affliction" (Deuteronomy 16:3), from the same root.

a: the eye of the land
p: A vivid Hebrew idiom for the visible surface of the ground.
b: 'Ein ha-arets, "the eye of the land," is the face of the ground as one sees it. The idiom appears only here, in 10:15 and in Numbers 22:5 and 22:11, where Balak says Israel "covers the eye of the land." A large desert locust swarm can hold billions of insects and blacken both sky and ground. Joel 2 pictures the Day of the LORD as just such an invasion.

a: Have you still not grasped that Egypt is lost?
p: Pharaoh's own court now pleads with him. His heart, and theirs, were "heavy" (10:1), yet they speak up.
b: God says he has made the servants' hearts heavy too (10:1), and yet here they urge Pharaoh to let Israel go. Interpreters handle this differently. Some say the hardening applies to the court only later, when they chase Israel to the sea (14:5). Others note that "heavy" hearts can still feel fear, but not yield. Literary readers see Pharaoh more and more isolated: magicians, officials and finally his own people are against him, until he is a lone figure crying "go" in the night (12:31).

a: With our young and with our old we will go
p: Pharaoh offers to release only the men. Moses insists the whole people, and their flocks, must go.
b: Pharaoh's bargaining shrinks step by step: worship in the land (8:25), not too far (8:28), men only (10:11), all but the flocks (10:24). Moses refuses every compromise. For Israel's worship, "a feast of the LORD," belongs to the whole community, children and elders, men and women. Later Jewish practice made this principle central: festivals such as Passover are kept by whole families, not only by priests or men. Pharaoh understands the real stakes: a people that leaves with its children and animals is not coming back.

a: there is evil right in front of your faces
p: Pharaoh's threat is obscure. Rashi heard the name of the sun god Ra, or a star called "Evil."
b: Ki ra'ah neged peneikhem may mean "you clearly have evil plans," or "evil is coming at you," a threat. Rashi, from the Midrash, says Pharaoh's astrologers saw a star called Ra'ah, "Evil," rising over Israel in the desert, a sign of blood and death; God later turned that blood into the blood of circumcision at Gilgal (Joshua 5:9). Some modern writers have suggested a pun on the Egyptian sun god Ra: "Ra is against you." No reading is certain.
orig: כִּי רָעָה נֶגֶד פְּנֵיכֶם (ki ra'ah neged peneikhem)

a: an east wind
p: An east wind brings the locusts; a west wind removes them. The same east wind will divide the sea.
b: Locust swarms do ride the winds; desert locusts from Arabia and Sudan are carried into Egypt by east and south winds. The east wind (ruach qadim) is the hot desert wind in the Bible (Genesis 41:6; Hosea 13:15). The "sea wind" of 10:19 is the west wind, since the Mediterranean lay west of Israel's writers. The same God-sent east wind will blow back the sea in 14:21. Supporters of natural explanations note how precisely the details fit the region; others stress that the wind comes and goes at Moses' word.

a: carry away my sin
p: Pharaoh uses the language of forgiveness: "lift away" his sin. Only God can do this.
b: "Forgive" in Hebrew is often nasa' chet, "to carry, lift up sin." Joseph's brothers used the same words to ask for Joseph's forgiveness (Genesis 50:17), and God is the one "forgiving guilt, rebellion and sin" (34:7), with the same verb. Pharaoh asks Moses to do it, and Moses brings the request to God. Later, the scapegoat "carries" Israel's sins away into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:22).

a: drove them into the Sea of Reeds
t: First mention of the Sea of Reeds
p: Yam Suf appears for the first time in Exodus here. Its location matters for the crossing story.
b: Yam Suf literally means "Sea of Reeds" (suf is the word for the reeds where Moses' basket lay, 2:3). The Septuagint translated it "Red Sea," the Greek name for the Red Sea and its gulfs, and English versions followed. In the Bible Yam Suf names the Gulf of Aqaba (1 Kings 9:26) and probably the Gulf of Suez (Numbers 33:10–11). Here, a west wind drives locusts out of Egypt into it, which fits a body east of the Delta. See the note on 13:18.

a: darkness over the land of Egypt
p: The ninth blow blots out Ra, Egypt's sun god, the chief god of the land. Some propose a sandstorm.
b: Ra (later Amun-Ra) was the supreme god of Egypt, and Pharaoh was called "son of Ra." Three days of darkness, while Israel has light, is the most direct assault on Egypt's religion. Natural explanations include the khamsin, a hot spring wind that can carry dust so thick it darkens the sky for days, or a dust storm after the vegetation was stripped. The text stresses a darkness so thick that people grope through it, while Israel's homes have light. Wisdom of Solomon 17–18 retells the scene with vivid moral imagery.
r: Genesis 1:2–4; Psalm 105:28; Isaiah 60:2; Amos 8:9; Mark 15:33; Revelation 16:10

a: Not one hoof will stay behind
t: "We do not know how we will serve"
p: Moses claims not to know which animals God will ask for. The whole herd must come.
b: Moses' answer is bold and witty: Israel cannot know what sacrifices God will require until they reach the mountain, so every animal must come. Some commentators admire his shrewdness; others see a deeper truth about worship.

a: Do not see my face again
t: "I will not see your face again"
p: Moses agrees he will not see Pharaoh again. Yet he speaks to him in chapter 11, and Pharaoh calls him in 12:31.
b: Several answers exist. (1) 11:4–8 is the continuation of this same meeting: Moses delivers the last warning before leaving "burning with anger" (11:8). Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it so. (2) In 12:31 Pharaoh "called" Moses, perhaps by messenger, not face to face; the Midrash has Pharaoh himself running through the streets at night looking for him. (3) Source critics assign 11:1–3 to a different strand, interrupting the scene.

a: he will drive you out from here completely, drive you right out
p: Moses asked Pharaoh to "send" Israel. In the end Pharaoh will not just send them, he will throw them out.
b: The key verb of the story has been shalach, "send away, let go." Now God adds garesh yegaresh, "he will surely drive you out," the word for expelling or divorcing. It was promised in 6:1 and comes true in 12:33 and 12:39, when the Egyptians hurry Israel out. Manetho's later story, preserved by Josephus, also speaks of an "expulsion" from Egypt, though in a very different, hostile version. "Completely" renders kalah; Rashi also allows "with everything," that is, with all your people and goods.

a: The man Moses was also held in high honor
p: The text pauses to say Moses was highly respected in Egypt. This explains why Egyptians gave freely.
b: "The man Moses" (ha-ish Moshe) is an unusual phrase, repeated in Numbers 12:3 ("the man Moses was very humble"). The verse explains the generous gifts of 12:35–36: the Egyptians gave not only from fear but because they had come to respect Moses. Many readers, ancient and modern, have felt that such praise sounds like a later narrator's comment rather than Moses writing about himself; the same was said of Numbers 12:3.

a: Around the middle of the night
p: Moses says "about midnight." The Talmud asks why he did not say exactly midnight.
b: Hebrew ka-chatsot ha-laylah means "about the middle of the night." In 12:29 the narrator says "in the middle of the night." The Talmud (Berakhot 3b–4a) explains that Moses knew the exact time but said "about," in case Pharaoh's astrologers miscounted and called him a liar. Midnight became a sacred time in Jewish piety: King David rose at midnight to praise God (Psalm 119:62). Jesus' parable of the bridegroom arriving "at midnight" (Matthew 25:6) draws on the same sense.

a: Every firstborn in the land of Egypt will die
p: The last blow kills Egypt's firstborn. Readers have long wrestled with its morality.
b: This is the hardest plague for modern readers. Several lines of response exist. (1) Measure for measure: Egypt killed Israel's sons (1:22), and Pharaoh was warned that God would take his firstborn for refusing to free God's "firstborn," Israel (4:22–23). (2) Pharaoh's choice: the blow came only after nine warnings. (3) Jewish practice softens the triumph: at the Seder, drops of wine are spilled for each plague, and the Talmud imagines God rebuking angels who wanted to sing while Egyptians drowned (Megillah 10b). (4) Critical and ethical readers (including some liberation and feminist critics) admit the text's violence and ask how it should shape readers today.

a: the slave woman at the hand mill
p: Grinding grain by hand was the lowest work in the ancient world, done by slave women and prisoners.
b: Egyptian statues show servants kneeling over a saddle quern, a flat stone on which grain was rubbed with a hand stone, hour after hour. The phrase covers all society, from the throne to the lowest worker. Compare Samson grinding in prison (Judges 16:21) and Jesus' words, "Two women will be grinding at the millstone" (Matthew 24:41). In 12:29 the parallel phrase is "the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon."

a: not a dog will sharpen its tongue
p: A proverb: Israel will be so safe that not even a dog will growl at them.
b: The Hebrew idiom lo yecheratz kelev leshono, "a dog will not sharpen (or point) its tongue," means total calm: on the night Egypt wails, not even a dog will snarl at Israel (compare Joshua 10:21). The Mekhilta says that God rewarded the dogs for their silence by giving them the torn meat that Israel may not eat (22:31). Some also suggest a play on the dog-headed Egyptian god Anubis, guardian of the dead, who is powerless that night.

a: so that my wonders will be many
p: The narrator gives a purpose for the long struggle: to multiply God's wonders, so all may know.
b: 11:9–10 sums up chapters 7–11, repeating 7:3–4. The question of why God did not free Israel at once runs through the story. The text's own answers: so Egypt and Israel will know the LORD (7:5; 10:2), so his name will be told in all the earth (9:16), and so Israel will tell its children. Terence Fretheim sees the plagues as creation itself fighting the chaos of Pharaoh's oppression; others stress the demonstration of the LORD's power over Egypt's gods (12:12).

a: This month will be the head of the months for you
p: The exodus month becomes Israel's first month. Jews still count months from spring but begin the year in autumn.
b: The month is called Abib (13:4), "fresh ears of grain," in spring (March–April); after the exile in Babylon it took the Babylonian name Nisan (Esther 3:7). Israel's religious calendar counts from this month, so the Day of Atonement falls in the seventh month (Leviticus 23). Yet Israel also knew an autumn new year, and the Gezer Calendar (about 900s BC) begins with the autumn harvest. Rabbinic law keeps both: Nisan is the first month for kings and festivals, Tishri the new year for years (Mishnah, Rosh Hashanah 1:1). Rashi opened his Torah commentary asking why the Torah did not begin here, with Israel's first command.

a: let them each take a lamb
p: The word seh means one animal of the flock, a lamb or a young goat (12:5).
b: Seh means a single head of small livestock, either sheep or goat, as 12:5 makes clear. English "Passover lamb" became standard because lambs were the usual choice and because of Christian imagery (John 1:29). Rabbinic tradition explained the four days between choosing and slaughtering as time to check the animal for flaws (Talmud, Pesachim 96a); it also places the selection on the day Israel would later enter Canaan (Joshua 4:19). Rabbinic law later made the tenth-day selection a rule for the first Passover only (Mishnah, Pesachim 9:5).

a: between the two evenings
p: An old Hebrew phrase for twilight. The Samaritans and rabbis differed on just when it is.
b: Bein ha-'arbayim is a dual form, "between the two evenings." The Samaritans and the Karaites (with Ibn Ezra) understood the time between sunset and full darkness. The Pharisees and the Mishnah understood the afternoon, from the sun's decline (about 3 PM) until sunset; this fits Josephus, who says the lambs were slaughtered from the ninth to the eleventh hour (Jewish War 6.423). The Samaritans still sacrifice Passover lambs at dusk on Mount Gerizim today. Christians noticed that Jesus died at about the ninth hour (Mark 15:34).

a: put it on the two doorposts and on the beam above the door
p: Many scholars think Passover grew from an older shepherds' rite that protected the camp. Others see it as new.
b: Critical scholars since Julius Wellhausen and Leonhard Rost have proposed that Passover began as a spring rite of herders, a night sacrifice to protect flocks and families from harm as they moved to new pasture; similar blood rites at tents and doors are known among Arab Bedouin. The Feast of Unleavened Bread may have been a separate farmers' festival, joined to Passover later (compare Deuteronomy 16). Traditional readers stress what the text says: the rite began at the exodus and is defined by it. Either way, Exodus gives the blood one meaning: a sign that the household belongs to the LORD. The mezuzah, a scroll on Jewish doorposts, uses the same word (Deuteronomy 6:9).

a: They will eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs
p: The three foods of the first Passover still sit at the center of the Jewish Seder.
b: Matzot (unleavened bread) and merorim (bitter herbs) join the roasted meat. Rabban Gamaliel taught, as the Mishnah records, that whoever has not explained three things at Passover has not done their duty: the Passover sacrifice, the matzah and the maror (Pesachim 10:5). Since the destruction of the Temple in AD 70, Jews no longer sacrifice the lamb; a roasted shank bone recalls it. The bitter herbs recall the bitter slavery (1:14), and the matzah the haste of leaving (12:39). Samaritans, who still sacrifice, keep the meal much as Exodus describes.

a: or boiled at all in water
p: Exodus requires roasting. Deuteronomy 16:7 seems to say "boil." Later Israel harmonized the two.
b: Here the meat must be roasted, not boiled. Deuteronomy 16:7 uses the verb bashal, usually "boil" or "cook." The Chronicler, describing Josiah's Passover, combines them: "They cooked the Passover in the fire, by the rule" (2 Chronicles 35:13), using Deuteronomy's verb with Exodus's fire. Rabbis read bashal in Deuteronomy as a general word for cooking, including roasting. Source critics see two traditions, an older home meal (here) and a later Temple rite (Deuteronomy). Either way the head, legs and inner parts are roasted whole, so the animal is not cut up.

a: It is a Passover to the LORD
p: Pesach may mean "pass over" or "protect." Both senses appear in ancient translations.
b: The noun pesach comes from the verb pasach in 12:13, 23 and 27. Most take it as "pass over, skip," as with a limping step (the same root in 1 Kings 18:21). But Isaiah 31:5 uses it alongside "shield" and "rescue": the LORD will "protect and save, spare and deliver Jerusalem." Targum Onkelos and the Mekhilta render 12:13 as "I will have pity on you," and some modern scholars favor "protect" or "stand guard over." The Greek pascha, borrowed from Aramaic, gave the Christian name for Easter in most languages (French Pâques, Spanish Pascua).

a: your waist wrapped for travel
p: Israel eats dressed for the road, robes tucked into belts. Jesus and Peter use the same image.
b: Long robes were tied up into a belt for work or travel, "girding the loins" in older English. Israel eats the first Passover ready to go at any moment; later Jews do not, since the Mishnah has them recline as free people (Pesachim 10:1). Jesus says, "Have your robes tucked into your belts and your lamps lit" (Luke 12:35), and 1 Peter tells believers to "tie up the robes of your mind" (1 Peter 1:13), both drawing on this night.

a: on all the gods of Egypt I will carry out judgments
p: The plagues are framed as a contest with Egypt's gods. Not every plague matches a known deity.
b: Numbers 33:4 repeats the claim: "On their gods, too, the LORD had carried out judgments." Interpreters have long matched plagues to gods: the Nile (Hapi), frogs (Heqet), cattle (Apis, Hathor), the sun (Ra) and Pharaoh himself, a god-king whose son dies. Supporters such as John Currid see a deliberate polemic. Cautious scholars, including Nahum Sarna, note that some links are forced (no Egyptian god of gnats is known), and the polemic is against Egypt's whole order rather than a god-by-god list. The Mekhilta imagines the idols themselves being broken that night.

a: you will get rid of the leaven in your houses
p: Jewish households still search the home for leaven by candlelight the night before Passover.
b: Se'or is sourdough starter; chamets is anything leavened. The Mishnah opens tractate Pesachim with the search for leaven by lamp on the evening of the fourteenth, and the custom of burning it the next morning continues today. Leaven becomes a symbol in the New Testament: Jesus warns against "the yeast of the Pharisees" (Mark 8:15; the Greek zymē is leaven), and Paul tells the Corinthians, "Clean out the old leaven, so you can be a new batch... For our Passover, Christ, has been slaughtered" (1 Corinthians 5:7). The rabbis also saw leaven as a symbol of the proud impulse within (Berakhot 17a).

a: will be cut off from Israel
p: Karet, "being cut off," is a penalty debated by the rabbis: exile, early death, or loss of the world to come.
b: Venikhretah ha-nefesh ha-hi, "that person will be cut off," first appears for refusing circumcision (Genesis 17:14); the Mishnah lists thirty-six offenses that carry this penalty (Keritot 1:1). It is not a court sentence; the rabbis understood it as a punishment by God: childlessness or early death (Talmud, Mo'ed Katan 28a) or, for Maimonides, the loss of the soul's share in the world to come. Modern scholars debate whether it once meant expulsion from the community or the end of a family line.

a: Take a bunch of hyssop
p: A small, bushy plant used to sprinkle blood and water. It appears at the cross in John 19:29.
b: Biblical ezov is probably Syrian marjoram (Origanum syriacum), whose hairy stems hold liquid well. It is used again to cleanse lepers (Leviticus 14:4), in the red heifer rite (Numbers 19:6) and in David's prayer: "Take away my sin with hyssop, and I will be pure" (Psalm 51:7). In John's Gospel, the soldiers lift a sponge of sour wine to Jesus "on hyssop" (John 19:29), a likely echo of Passover; Hebrews 9:19 recalls hyssop at the covenant ceremony.
r: Leviticus 14:4–6; Numbers 19:6; Numbers 19:18; Psalm 51:7; John 19:29; Hebrews 9:19

a: the basin
p: Saf can mean a basin or a threshold. If threshold, the blood marked all four sides of the door.
b: Saf means "basin" in some places (2 Samuel 17:28) and "threshold" in others (Judges 19:27). The Septuagint here says the blood "by the door" and the Vulgate "on the threshold" (in limine), and some ancient and modern scholars agree: the lamb was slaughtered at the threshold, and its blood marked the lintel, two posts and the step. The Mekhilta records both views. Most English versions say "basin," which the Plain follows.

a: the destroyer
p: Is the destroyer the LORD himself, an angel, or a demon held back? The text seems to say both.
b: 12:12 and 12:29 say the LORD himself struck the firstborn; this verse speaks of ha-mashchit, "the destroyer," whom the LORD does not allow in. The Haggadah insists: "I and not an angel... I and not a messenger." Others identify the destroyer with the destroying angel of 2 Samuel 24:16 and 1 Chronicles 21:15; Hebrews 11:28 speaks of "the one who destroyed the firstborn." Critical scholars see a trace of an older belief in a night demon kept out by blood, absorbed into faith in one God.

a: What is this service to you?
p: The Torah expects children to ask. The Haggadah turns the four "children" passages into four sons.
b: Four times the Torah speaks of a child asking or being told about the exodus (here; 13:8; 13:14; Deuteronomy 6:20). The Haggadah reads them as four types of children: the wise, the wicked, the simple, and the one who does not know how to ask. It reads this verse as the wicked son, because he says "to you" and not "to us," setting himself outside the community. The Mishnah (Pesachim 10:4) prescribes that the child ask, and from this comes the Seder's "Why is this night different?"

a: the captive in the pit-house
p: The "house of the pit" is a prison, like the one Joseph knew. The blow reaches all ranks.
b: Beit ha-bor, "the house of the pit," is a dungeon: Joseph called his prison "the pit" (Genesis 40:15; 41:14). 11:5 said "the slave woman behind the hand mill"; here it is the prisoner. Rashi asks why prisoners' sons should suffer, and answers that the prisoners had rejoiced at Israel's slavery, or that they might claim their own gods had saved them. Modern readers note simply that the narrator means every household.

a: And bless me too
p: Pharaoh, defeated, asks for a blessing, just as an earlier Pharaoh was blessed by Jacob.
b: Jacob blessed Pharaoh twice when he arrived in Egypt (Genesis 47:7, 47:10), and God's promise to Abraham was that "all the clans of the earth will find blessing" in him (Genesis 12:3). This Pharaoh, after cursing Israel, asks Moses for a blessing as Israel leaves. The story comes full circle: Israel entered as guests bringing blessing and leaves with a broken king begging for one.

a: So they stripped Egypt bare
p: Was taking Egypt's gold just? Ancient answers range from back wages to a model for using pagan learning.
b: Vayenatsselu is a war word, "they plundered," fulfilling Genesis 15:14. Philo (Life of Moses 1.141) called it the wages owed for years of unpaid labor; the Talmud (Sanhedrin 91a) tells of a Jewish advocate before Alexander the Great who answered Egypt's claim for the gold by asking for 430 years of wages. Augustine (On Christian Teaching 2.40) made "the spoils of Egypt" a model for Christians using the best of pagan learning for God, a theme Origen had also used. The same gold later goes into both the golden calf and the sanctuary (32:2–4; 35:22).

a: about six hundred thousand men on foot
p: 600,000 men implies over two million people. Many scholars think "thousand" once meant a smaller unit.
b: With women and children, 600,000 men (Numbers 1:46 gives 603,550) suggests two to three million people, close to the whole estimated population of Egypt at the time (about 2.5 to 4.5 million), and a column many miles long. Literal readers accept the number as a miracle of provision. Others, following Flinders Petrie and George Mendenhall, argue that 'elef, "thousand," also means a clan or military unit, so "600 units" might be a few thousand fighters; Colin Humphreys works out about 20,000 people in all. Critical scholars often see a census from the time of the monarchy projected back, or a symbolic number.

a: from Rameses toward Succoth
p: Rameses is Pi-Ramesses near Qantir; Succoth is probably Tjeku, in the Wadi Tumilat.
b: Rameses is almost certainly Pi-Ramesses, the Delta capital built by Ramesses II near modern Qantir, over the ruins of the Hyksos city Avaris (see 1:11). Succoth, "booths," probably renders Egyptian Tjeku, a district in the Wadi Tumilat around Tell el-Maskhuta, eastward toward the Bitter Lakes. Papyrus Anastasi VI, a border report of about 1200 BC, tells of herders from Edom allowed past "the fortress of Merneptah in Tjeku" to the pools of Pithom. Those who date the exodus to 1446 BC take "Rameses" as a later name for the older site.

a: A large mixed crowd
p: Israel did not leave alone. Non-Israelites came too, and the text welcomes them into Passover (12:48).
b: 'Erev rav, "a large mixture," are people of other origins: Egyptians who feared the LORD (9:20), other slaves, or Semites in the Delta. Numbers 11:4 blames the "rabble" (asafsuf) among them for craving meat, and later Jewish tradition sometimes blamed the mixed crowd for the golden calf (Rashi on 32:7). But this chapter immediately gives a way for outsiders to join fully (12:48–49). Many historians think early Israel did form from mixed groups; liberation readers stress that the exodus was a people of the oppressed.

a: a night of keeping watch for the LORD
p: The LORD kept watch over Israel that night; Israel keeps watch every year. Targums say four great nights.
b: Leil shimmurim, "night of watchings," appears only here. The LORD watched to bring Israel out, and so Israel must watch, "guard" the night each year. The Palestinian Targums (Neofiti, Pseudo-Jonathan) expand the verse into a poem of "four nights" written in the Book of Memorials: creation, the covenant with Abraham, the exodus, and the night of final redemption when the Messiah will come. Christians kept a similar all-night vigil before Easter from early times.

a: no foreigner may eat it
p: An outsider (ben-nekhar) may not eat, but a resident foreigner (ger) who is circumcised may.
b: The law distinguishes three outsiders. A ben-nekhar, "son of foreignness," a non-Israelite who keeps his own identity, may not eat. A toshav or sakhir, a temporary settler or hired worker, may not either. But a bought slave who is circumcised may, and so may a ger, a resident foreigner who chooses to keep the feast and circumcises his males: "he will be like a native of the land" (12:48). The line is not race but covenant. In later Judaism, the ger became the convert.

a: do not break any of its bones
p: John's Gospel quotes this rule when soldiers do not break Jesus' legs on the cross.
b: The rule may have kept the meal whole, one animal for one community, or it may have marked the lamb as holy, not to be treated like ordinary meat. John reports that the soldiers broke the legs of the men crucified beside Jesus but not his, and adds: "This took place to fulfill the Scripture, 'No bone of his will be crushed'" (John 19:36, compare Numbers 9:12; Psalm 34:20). John also places Jesus' death on the day of preparation, when Passover lambs were slaughtered (John 19:14).

a: One law will hold
p: The first time torah, "teaching, law," appears in Exodus. Insider and resident foreigner are equal under it.
b: Torah achat, "one law" (literally "one instruction"), is the first use of torah in Exodus, the word that will name the five books of Moses. Its first application is equality: "one law for the native and for the foreigner who lives among you." The principle recurs in Leviticus 24:22 and Numbers 15:15–16. Michael Walzer and other political writers have read the exodus as the founding story of a people bound by law rather than by blood.

a: Set apart for me as holy every firstborn
p: Because God spared Israel's firstborn, they belong to him. Jews still "redeem" a firstborn son today.
b: The firstborn of Israel, spared on the night Egypt's firstborn died, are now God's own. Firstborn animals were to be sacrificed; firstborn sons were "ransomed" (13:13). Later the Levites take the place of Israel's firstborn in God's service (Numbers 3:11–13, 40–51), and five shekels are paid for each extra firstborn. The Jewish ceremony pidyon ha-ben, "redemption of the son," still pays five silver coins to a priest's descendant thirty days after a firstborn's birth. Luke tells how Mary and Joseph took Jesus up to Jerusalem "to present him to the Lord," following "what stands written in the law of the Lord" (Luke 2:22–23).

a: out of the house of slaves
p: Egypt is called "the house of slaves," a phrase that will open the Ten Commandments.
b: Beit 'avadim, "house of slaves" (KJV "house of bondage"), describes Egypt as one great slave quarters. It returns in the first words of the Ten Commandments: "I am the LORD your God. I brought you out of the land of Egypt, that house of slaves" (20:2). The phrase becomes a refrain in Deuteronomy and the prophets (Deuteronomy 5:6; Micah 6:4), reminding Israel that its God is defined by the act of freeing slaves.

a: It is because of this
p: The Haggadah reads "this" as pointing to the matzah and bitter herbs on the table.
b: "Because of this" (ba'avur zeh) seems to point to something visible. The Haggadah draws the rule that the story must be told "at the time when matzah and maror are placed before you," that is, at the Seder. It also notes that the parent says "for me": each generation tells the story as its own. Some interpreters, like Ibn Ezra, read the phrase in reverse: "we keep this rite because of what the LORD did." Christian worship has a similar logic of remembering: "Do this to remember me" (Luke 22:19).

a: a sign on your hand for you and a reminder between your eyes
p: Jews bind small scrolls of this passage on arm and head. Some interpreters read the verse as a figure of speech.
b: Four passages speak of a sign on the hand and between the eyes (here; 13:16; Deuteronomy 6:8; 11:18). Rabbinic Judaism reads them literally: tefillin, leather boxes holding these four texts, are bound on the arm and forehead at weekday morning prayer (Talmud, Menachot 34b–37b). Tefillin from the first century BC were found at Qumran, and Jesus mentions phylacteries (Matthew 23:5). Rashbam, Rashi's grandson, said the plain sense is a metaphor, like "Keep them tied to your heart" in Proverbs 6:21 (compare 3:3): let the memory be as close as something you wear. Karaite Jews and Samaritans also read it figuratively.
r: 13:16; Deuteronomy 6:8; Deuteronomy 11:18; Proverbs 3:3; Proverbs 6:21; Song of Songs 8:6; Matthew 23:5

a: Every first to open the womb of a donkey you will ransom with a lamb
p: The donkey, an "unclean" animal, could not be sacrificed, so it was bought back with a lamb.
b: Donkeys were the working trucks of the ancient world but could not be offered on the altar. So a lamb was given in place of a firstborn donkey; if the owner refused, the donkey had to be killed, so that no one profited from what belonged to God. The rabbis said the donkey was singled out because donkeys carried Egypt's riches out with Israel (Talmud, Bekhorot 5b), and they still practice the rite (peter chamor). The word for "ransom," padah, means to buy back by paying a price.

a: Pharaoh made it hard for himself
p: Here the hardening verb qashah is used with Pharaoh as the one who did it, not God.
b: Looking back, the father explains to his son: ki hiqshah Far'oh, "when Pharaoh made it hard" to let Israel go. The verb is the same qashah used of God in 7:3. In the retelling for children, the responsibility is put plainly on Pharaoh. Readers who see a balance between God's action and Pharaoh's choice often point to verses like this.

a: a band between your eyes
p: The rare word totafot may mean a headband or an ornament. The Talmud found it puzzling too.
b: In 13:9 the parallel word is zikkaron, "reminder." Here it is totafot, which occurs only here and in Deuteronomy 6:8 and 11:18. The Talmud (Menachot 34b; Sanhedrin 4b) explained it as a word from two foreign languages, each meaning "two," thus four compartments of the head tefillin. Modern scholars connect it with a headband or forehead pendant, like ornaments worn in the ancient Near East for protection or remembrance.

a: by way of the Philistines' land
p: The coast road to Canaan was guarded by Egyptian forts. But the Philistines arrived only around 1175 BC.
b: The shortest route from the Delta to Canaan ran along the coast, called in Egyptian texts the "Ways of Horus." A relief of Seti I at Karnak shows its chain of forts and wells, and James Hoffmeier excavated one of them at Tell el-Borg. An army of runaway slaves would meet Egyptian troops at once: hence "when they see fighting." The name "Philistines," however, belongs to the Sea Peoples who settled the coast about 1175 BC. Critical scholars take it as a sign of a later writer; traditional scholars say the later name was used for the reader's sake, as a modern map says "Israel" for ancient Canaan.

a: by the wilderness road to the Sea of Reeds
p: Did Israel cross a marshy lake on Egypt's border, the Gulf of Suez, or the Gulf of Aqaba? Each has defenders.
b: The names in 14:2 are not securely located, so there are several proposals. (1) A northern lake, such as Lake Sirbonis on the Mediterranean coast (Otto Eissfeldt) or Lake Ballah, near the line of forts. (2) Lake Timsah or the Bitter Lakes, reed-filled waters along the Suez isthmus (Hoffmeier, Kitchen). (3) The Gulf of Suez, the traditional view, and the sense of the Greek "Red Sea." (4) The Gulf of Aqaba, sometimes linked with placing Sinai in Arabia (Galatians 4:25), and favored by Colin Humphreys and some popular writers. Bernard Batto argues that Yam Suf also carried the mythic sense "Sea of the End." Critical scholars often think the tradition kept no exact location.

a: in battle order
p: Chamushim may mean "armed," "in battle ranks," or "in fives." A Midrash says only one in five left Egypt.
b: Chamushim appears also in Joshua 1:14 and 4:12 for warriors crossing the Jordan "armed" or "in formation." It may come from chamesh, "five," referring to an army's five divisions. Onkelos says "armed." A Midrash quoted by Rashi reads "one in five": only a fifth of Israel left Egypt, and the rest died in the darkness because they did not want to go. Other rabbis said one in fifty or one in five hundred. The Septuagint read the word differently, as "in the fifth generation" (see the variant). The Plain follows the military sense.

a: Moses took Joseph's bones with him
p: Joseph's dying request in Genesis is kept. The bones are buried at Shechem in Joshua 24:32.
b: Genesis ends with Joseph saying, "God will surely come to help you... carry my bones up from here" (Genesis 50:24–25). His coffin waited in Egypt for four hundred years. The Talmud (Sotah 13a) praises Moses for busying himself with Joseph's bones while everyone else was busy with gold. The bones travel through the whole wilderness and are buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32). Hebrews 11:22 counts Joseph's instruction as an act of faith.

a: by day in a pillar of cloud
t: The pillar of cloud and fire
p: God's presence leads Israel as cloud by day and fire by night. Some compare an army's signal brazier.
b: The pillar is the LORD's visible presence: "the LORD was walking in front of them." It will guard the sea (14:19–20), fill the Tabernacle (40:34–38) and guide the march (Numbers 9:15–23). Later Jewish tradition called God's dwelling presence the Shekhinah. Some scholars compare ancient armies, which carried a brazier on a pole at the head of the march, smoke by day and fire by night, or think of a volcano seen from afar. Paul says Israel was "baptized into Moses by the cloud and the sea" (1 Corinthians 10:1–2), and Isaiah pictures the cloud and fire over a renewed Zion (Isaiah 4:5).

a: to turn back
p: Israel turns back to camp near three named places. Each has been located in more than one place.
b: Migdol means "tower, fort" and is a known Egyptian border fort name; Egyptian texts mention more than one, and one near Pelusium has been identified at Tell Kedua. Baal-zephon, "Lord of the North," was a Canaanite storm god also worshiped in the Delta, with a shrine near Lake Sirbonis (Mount Casius) and possibly another near Tahpanhes. Pi-hahiroth may be Egyptian for "house of Hathor" or Semitic "mouth of the canals." The command to "turn back" is meant to make Israel look lost (14:3), luring Pharaoh. Rashi, following the Mekhilta, says Baal-zephon was the one idol God left standing, so Egypt would think its god had trapped Israel.

a: I will win glory for myself through Pharaoh
p: "Win glory" is from kaved, the root of Pharaoh's "heavy" heart. God will be "weighty" through Pharaoh.
b: Ve'ikkavedah, "I will get glory, be honored," is from kaved, "heavy, weighty," the same root used for Pharaoh's heavy heart (7:14; 8:15) and for the "heavy" plagues (9:3, 18, 24). The writer plays on it: Pharaoh made his heart heavy against God, and now God will make his own weight, his glory, felt through Pharaoh. The kavod, "glory," of the LORD will later fill the Tabernacle (40:34). The Plain cannot keep the pun, but this note can.

a: six hundred chosen chariots
p: Light two-man war chariots were the pride of the New Kingdom army.
b: Egypt adopted the horse-drawn war chariot from western Asia in the Hyksos period and made it the core of its army in the New Kingdom (about 1550–1070 BC). Each light chariot carried a driver and a warrior with bow or spear, the "officers" (shalishim) may be a third man or an elite rank. At the battle of Kadesh, Ramesses II claimed to face 2,500 Hittite chariots. Six hundred is a large but credible strike force. The number matches Israel's "six hundred thousand" (12:37): an elite force against a crowd of slaves.

a: with a hand raised high
p: Beyad ramah means openly and defiantly. Targum Onkelos says "with heads uncovered," like free people.
b: Beyad ramah is a gesture of power and boldness. Numbers 33:3 repeats it of the exodus; Numbers 15:30 uses it for sinning "with a high hand," defiantly and on purpose. Israel does not sneak away but leaves in plain sight. Targum Onkelos turns it into beresh gelei, "with uncovered head," a sign of freedom and confidence, since slaves and mourners covered their heads. The image of the LORD's raised hand and outstretched arm is also an Egyptian royal image (Hoffmeier).

a: Were there no graves in Egypt
p: A bitter joke: Egypt, the land of tombs and pyramids, had no graves to spare?
b: Egypt was famous for its tombs; its whole civilization was organized around burial. The people's sarcasm is the first of many complaints in the wilderness (15:24; 16:2–3; 17:3), a pattern sometimes called the "murmuring" stories. Their words "what is this you have done to us" also mirror Pharaoh's "what is this we have done" (14:5, literally): both sides regret the exodus on the same night.

a: The LORD will fight for you. And you? You will keep quiet.
p: Israel does nothing in the battle. A Midrash pictures four groups at the sea with four different plans.
b: The Mekhilta and the Jerusalem Targums describe Israel split four ways at the shore: some wanted to drown themselves, some to go back to Egypt, some to fight, and some to shout and pray. Moses answers each in 14:13–14: "do not be afraid... take your stand... you will never see them again... the LORD will fight for you... keep quiet." The idea that the LORD alone wins became central to Israel's theology of holy war (Deuteronomy 1:30; 2 Chronicles 20:15–17). Isaiah: "Your strength will come from being calm and trusting" (Isaiah 30:15).

a: Why cry out to me?
p: God rebukes Moses for praying when it is time to act. A famous Midrash has a man walk into the sea first.
b: Moses has not been said to cry out, which puzzled readers; perhaps he prayed silently, or the verse speaks to Israel through him. The Talmud (Sotah 37a) tells that the tribes argued over who should go in first until Nahshon son of Amminadab of Judah jumped into the sea, which rose to his nose before it parted; Moses was praying at length, and God said, "My beloved ones are drowning, and you pray?" Judah's leadership was explained by this. The verse is often quoted to teach that faith must sometimes move.

a: The angel of God
p: The angel of God and the pillar of cloud both move behind Israel. Two sources, or one presence?
b: The verse says two parallel things: the angel moved behind, and the pillar moved behind. Source critics often assign the angel to E and the pillar to J, combined here. Traditional readers take them as two descriptions of one presence: the angel is God's messenger who is also God himself (see 3:2; 23:20–23). Rashi notes that the angel moved to take the arrows and stones of the Egyptians. Christians from Justin Martyr on often saw in this angel the Son of God before his birth.

a: the LORD made the sea go back by a fierce east wind
p: Computer models show a strong wind can push water off a shallow lagoon. Others insist on a purely divine act.
b: The text says God used a wind blowing all night. In 2010 Carl Drews and Weiqing Han modeled how a steady wind of about 63 mph over twelve hours could expose a land bridge in the eastern Nile Delta near the old Lake of Tanis, a "wind setdown." Colin Humphreys proposed a similar effect at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, and others have suggested a tsunami from the Thera eruption. Many believers are glad to see God working through nature, with the miracle in the timing. Others note that 14:22 and 15:8 describe walls of water standing up, which no wind explains. Critical scholars see two versions combined: a wind that dries the sea (J) and a sea split by Moses' hand (P).

a: the water standing as a wall for them
p: The crossing echoes creation's dry land and anticipates the Jordan, baptism and the new exodus.
b: Dry land appearing from parted waters recalls the third day of creation (Genesis 1:9) and the flood's end (Genesis 8:13). Israel will cross the Jordan in the same way (Joshua 3–4), and Elijah and Elisha repeat it (2 Kings 2:8, 14). Psalm 114 makes the sea a character: "The sea looked and ran away" (114:3). Isaiah promises a new exodus: "I will be with you when you go through the waters" (Isaiah 43:2, 16). Paul calls the crossing a baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1–2), and the early church read this chapter at the Easter vigil, as many churches still do.
r: 15:8; Genesis 1:9; Genesis 8:13; Joshua 3:13–17; 2 Kings 2:8; Isaiah 43:16; Isaiah 51:10; 1 Corinthians 10:1–2; Hebrews 11:29; Psalm 114:3–5; Isaiah 11:15–16

a: In the morning watch
p: The last third of the night, before dawn. Ancient armies often attacked at this hour.
b: Israel divided the night into three watches (Judges 7:19; Lamentations 2:19); the morning watch ran from about 2 AM to sunrise. Gideon and Saul both attacked at this time (Judges 7:19; 1 Samuel 11:11). God "looks down" through the pillar of fire and cloud, and the panic (vayyaham) that seizes Egypt is the same divine terror sent on Israel's enemies in holy war (23:27; Joshua 10:10).

a: the LORD shook Egypt off into the middle of the sea
p: Na'ar is to shake out, as one shakes dust from a cloth.
b: Vayna'er pictures the LORD shaking the Egyptians off, like crumbs from a garment or a lap (Nehemiah 5:13; Psalm 109:23; Isaiah 33:9). The Egyptians are fleeing toward the returning water, a picture of total confusion. The "full strength" of the sea (le'eitano) means it returned to its normal state, the Hebrew word for "constant, ever-flowing."

a: Not one of them was left, not even one
p: Exodus never says Pharaoh himself died. A Midrash says he survived and became king of Nineveh.
b: The text says all the army that entered the sea drowned. Psalm 136:15 says God "shook Pharaoh and his army off into the Sea of Reeds." Whether Pharaoh personally died is left open. Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer (43) says he survived to bear witness and later ruled Nineveh, where he repented at Jonah's preaching. The Qur'an says Pharaoh professed faith as he drowned, and that his body was saved as a sign (Surah 10:90–92). No known Egyptian king's mummy shows death by drowning; this is often cited against identifying a particular Pharaoh with the story.

a: So on that day the LORD saved Israel from the hand of Egypt
p: The first time the Bible says the LORD "saved" Israel. Psalms, Joshua and Jude look back to this day.
b: Vayyosha', "and he saved," is from the root of yeshu'ah, "salvation" (14:13; 15:2), and of the names Joshua and Jesus. Joshua's farewell retells the darkness between the camps and the drowning (Joshua 24:5–7), and Psalm 106:8–10 says God saved them "for his name's sake." Jude 5 reminds readers that the Lord, having saved a people out of Egypt, later destroyed those who did not believe; some important manuscripts there read "Jesus" for "the Lord," a famous variant.

a: They believed in the LORD and in Moses his servant
t: Faith in God and his servant
p: The chapter ends with faith, the first since 4:31, and prepares for the song.
b: "They believed" (vaya'aminu) recalls Abraham, who "put his trust in the LORD" (Genesis 15:6), and Israel's first trust at 4:31. Faith here is linked with both God and his chosen servant, a pairing that returns at Sinai (19:9). The Mekhilta, on 15:1, comments: "By the merit of faith Israel was redeemed, and by the merit of faith they sang." The "great hand" (ha-yad ha-gedolah) closes the many references to God's hand throughout the story. Hebrews 11:29 credits the crossing to faith, and Hebrews 3:5 recalls Moses as faithful "as a servant" in God's house.
r: 4:31; 19:9; Genesis 15:6; Numbers 14:11; Psalm 106:12; John 5:46; Hebrews 11:29; Hebrews 3:5

a: Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to the LORD
t: How old is the Song of the Sea?
p: Many scholars consider this among the oldest poems in the Bible. Others date it to the time of the Temple or later.
b: Early date: Frank Moore Cross and David Noel Freedman ("The Song of Miriam," 1955; reprinted 1975) argued from archaic grammar and spelling, such as the old endings in yechasyumu, "cover them" (15:5), and from its kinship with Ugaritic poetry, that the song dates to the 1100s BC or earlier; Brian Russell and others broadly agree. Later date: others point to 15:17, which seems to know the Jerusalem Temple, and suggest the monarchy or later, with archaic style used on purpose. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take it as Moses' song at the sea. Many agree it is older than the prose story around it. The Song is written in the Torah scroll in a special brick-like pattern (Talmud, Megillah 16b).

a: for he has risen up high, so high
p: Ga'oh ga'ah: "he has risen up, he has risen up." The doubled verb is like a shout of triumph.
b: Ki ga'oh ga'ah doubles the verb for emphasis, as Hebrew often does: "truly he has risen up." The root is used of the sea's waves rising (Job 38:11) and of proud people (Isaiah 2:12). God rises up over the proud Pharaoh. The Mekhilta lists ways God is "exalted" above human kings. Older versions said "he has triumphed gloriously" (KJV); the Plain keeps the doubled sound.

a: Horse and its rider
p: Egypt had very little cavalry. "Rider" may mean the man in the chariot.
b: Cavalry, men riding horses into battle, became common only after about 900 BC; Egypt's army fought from chariots. Rokhev, "rider," can mean one who rides in a chariot (2 Kings 9:16; Jeremiah 51:21), so "horse and its driver" is possible. Some critics see the image of riders as a sign of a later date; others say poetry uses the words loosely. The line is also Miriam's song (15:21), probably the oldest form.

a: My strength and my song is Yah
p: "Yah" is a short form of God's name. The line is quoted in Isaiah 12:2 and Psalm 118:14.
b: Yah is a short form of YHWH, the first time it appears in the Bible; it lives on in Hallelu-yah, "praise Yah." Zimrat, "song," is unusual; some scholars, comparing Arabic and Ugaritic, read "my strength and my protection" or "my might." The whole line is repeated word for word in Isaiah 12:2 and Psalm 118:14, so it was a well-known confession. The KJV renders it "The LORD is my strength and song."

a: This is my God, and I will honor him
p: The rabbis said even a servant girl at the sea saw God more clearly than later prophets did.
b: The word "this" (zeh) suggests pointing. The Mekhilta says that at the sea a maidservant saw what the prophet Ezekiel never saw: they could point and say, "This is my God." The verb anvehu, "I will honor him," is rare. Onkelos translates it "I will build him a sanctuary" (from naveh, "dwelling"). The Talmud (Shabbat 133b) reads it as "I will beautify him," making beautiful objects for God's commandments, and also as "I will be like him": as he is gracious, so be gracious.

a: The LORD is a man of war
p: The LORD as warrior is an ancient image. It troubles many readers and comforted the oppressed.
b: Ish milchamah, "a man of war," pictures the LORD as a warrior, an image shared with Canaanite poems about Baal. The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint soften it (see the variant). Onkelos says "the master of victories." Marcion in the second century rejected this "warrior" God, and Tertullian answered him. Liberation and Black theologians such as James Cone saw in the warrior God the defender of slaves against their masters; others warn how such texts have been used to justify violence.

a: sank down in the Sea of Reeds
t: Sea of Reeds, sea of the end
p: The poem's Yam Suf is the same name as in the prose. The Greek and most English versions say "Red Sea."
b: This is the first Yam Suf in poetry. The Septuagint's "Red Sea" (Erythra Thalassa) is how Greek speakers named the whole sea south and east of Egypt, including the Gulfs of Suez and Aqaba. Bernard Batto suggested suf here also echoes sof, "end," the sea at the edge of the world, giving the scene a cosmic tone. Many scholars think the original tradition spoke of a reedy marsh; others defend a real gulf. See the note at 13:18.

a: The deeps cover them
p: Tehomot, "the deeps," is the word for the primal waters of Genesis 1:2. The sea serves its Creator.
b: Tehom, the deep, is the dark ocean of Genesis 1:2. In Babylonian myth Tiamat, the sea monster, is slain by the storm god Marduk, and in Canaanite myth Baal defeats Yam, "Sea." Here the sea is not God's enemy but his weapon: the enemy is Pharaoh. Psalm 74:12–15 and Isaiah 51:9–10 combine the creation battle and the sea crossing: "Wasn't it you who dried the sea, the waters of the vast deep?" The archaic verb ending here (yechasyumu) is one sign of the song's age.

a: the waters were heaped up
p: The poem pictures standing walls of water. Some think the prose took its "walls" from this poetry.
b: Ne'ermu mayim, "waters piled up," and nitsevu khemo ned, "stood like a heap," paint the sea as frozen in place; qafe'u, "went stiff," is used of curdled milk (Job 10:10). Some scholars think the poem is older and that the prose "wall" (14:22) took up its images. Others say poetry and prose describe the same event in two registers. Either way, "the wind from your nostrils" is the east wind of 14:21 described as God's breath.

a: I'll chase, I'll catch
p: Six short verbs in a row, gasping with greed. The Hebrew sounds like a man out of breath.
b: The enemy's speech is six verbs, each one word in Hebrew: erdof, assig, achallek shalal, timla'emo nafshi, ariq charbi, torishemo yadi, with heavy "i" and "a" sounds. Readers have long admired its sound: the breathless, greedy boast of the hunter, which the next verse answers with one breath of God. "Glutted" is nefesh, the soul or appetite.

a: Like lead they went under
p: Lead was well known in Egypt and Canaan. It sinks fast, a vivid picture of armored soldiers.
b: Lead (oferet) was mined and used in Egypt from early times for weights, net sinkers and small objects. Fishermen tied lead to their nets so they would sink quickly, which may stand behind the simile. In 15:5 they went down "like a stone"; here "like lead," two quick, heavy images. The Mekhilta notes three images in the song: stubble (15:7), stone (15:5) and lead (15:10), and says each matches different groups among the Egyptians.

a: Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?
p: This verse is sung in every Jewish evening and morning service, right after the Shema.
b: Mi khamokha ba'elim YHWH is one of the best-known lines in Jewish prayer. It belongs to the blessing after the Shema, the Ge'ulah, "redemption," sung morning and evening, joined with 15:18. "Among the gods" assumes other heavenly beings and rival gods, the language of the divine council (Psalm 82:1; 89:6–8), without granting them equal power. A famous tradition says the Maccabees' name came from the initials of this line (M-K-B-Y), though most historians derive it from maqqaba, "hammer."

a: The earth swallowed them
p: Why "earth" when they drowned? Erets may mean the underworld, the realm of the dead.
b: The enemy drowned in the sea, yet the earth swallows them. In poetry erets, "earth," can mean the underworld (Jonah 2:6; Psalm 71:20), as Akkadian ersetu does, so the sea becomes the gateway to death. The Mekhilta explains that the earth received the bodies only after the sea cast them out (14:30), as a reward for Pharaoh's admission, "The LORD is the righteous one" (9:27). The same verb "swallow" was used of Aaron's staff (7:12).

a: You led on in your loyal love
p: The first hesed in Exodus: God's faithful, committed love for the people he has redeemed.
b: Chesed is covenant love: steady kindness owed and given within a bond. English has no single word for it (KJV "mercy," others "steadfast love" or "unfailing love"). It is linked here with ga'alta, "you redeemed," the act of a kinsman who rescues family (6:6). The verbs move to the future: God leads and guides them to his neveh, a shepherd's pasture and dwelling, probably meaning the land or the sanctuary.

a: those who live in Philistia
p: The nations listed fit the conquest era as Israel's later story tells it. Philistia raises a dating question.
b: The song names Philistia, Edom, Moab and Canaan, roughly in the order Israel will meet them in Numbers and Joshua: Edom and Moab refuse passage (Numbers 20–22), and Rahab tells the spies that "all who live in the land melt" before Israel (Joshua 2:9–11), repeating 15:15. Since the Philistines settled the coast only about 1175 BC, some date the song after that; others see it as a natural name for the coast in a poem sung for generations. The "chiefs" of Edom (allufim) is the title used for Edom's clan chiefs in Genesis 36.

a: until this people you have made your own cross over
p: Qanita means "you acquired, created." The same verb is used of God "creating" heaven and earth.
b: Am zu qanita, "this people you have acquired," uses qanah, which means "buy" or "acquire" (Genesis 25:10) and also "create, bring into being": Eve's "I have gained a man" (Genesis 4:1) and "God Most High, maker of heaven and earth" (Genesis 14:19). Deuteronomy 32:6 combines the senses: "Isn't he your father, who brought you into being?" The repeated "until they cross over" may point to the Jordan, the second crossing.

a: on the mountain that is your own
p: Sinai, the whole hill country of Canaan, or Mount Zion in Jerusalem? The answer affects the song's date.
b: Har nachalatekha, "the mountain of your inheritance," with "your throne" and "sanctuary" (miqdash), sounds like the Jerusalem Temple (Psalm 78:54, 68–69). Those who date the song late see Zion here. Cross and Freedman compared Ugaritic poems in which Baal's mountain Zaphon is "the mountain of my inheritance," and argued the phrase can mean the land of Canaan as God's mountain home, or a sanctuary like Shiloh. Traditional readers take it as prophecy of the Temple. Rashi, reading "your hands set firm," says the earthly sanctuary corresponds to a heavenly one.

a: The LORD will be king forever and ever
p: The first time the Bible calls God "king." The line closes the redemption blessing in Jewish prayer.
b: YHWH yimlokh le'olam va'ed is the first explicit statement in Scripture that the LORD reigns as king. After defeating Pharaoh, a god-king, the LORD is proclaimed the true king. Jewish liturgy repeats it after Mi khamokha each day. The Targums expand: "The LORD, his kingdom stands forever." Psalms 93–99 sing "the LORD reigns"; Revelation 11:15 announces that "he will rule forever and ever."
orig: יְהוָה יִמְלֹךְ לְעֹלָם וָעֶד (YHWH yimlokh le'olam va'ed)

a: Miriam the prophet
p: The first woman called a prophet in the Bible. Many scholars think her short song is the older original.
b: Miriam is the first woman called nevi'ah, "prophetess," followed by Deborah, Huldah and others. Micah names her with Moses and Aaron as Israel's leaders (Micah 6:4). Women leading victory songs with drums and dances is well attested (Judges 11:34; 1 Samuel 18:6–7). Frank Cross and other scholars proposed that the whole song was once called the Song of Miriam, and that later tradition gave it to Moses. A Qumran manuscript (4Q365) preserves extra lines of a Song of Miriam. Feminist readers such as Phyllis Trible and J. Cheryl Exum have highlighted her role.
r: 2:4–8; Numbers 12:1–15; Numbers 20:1; Judges 4:4; 2 Kings 22:14; Micah 6:4; Luke 2:36

a: hand drum
p: The tof is a frame drum played mostly by women, not the tambourine with jingles.
b: The tof is a round frame drum, a skin stretched over a wooden ring. Figurines from Israel and Phoenicia in the Iron Age show women holding such drums at the shoulder, and Carol Meyers has argued that frame drum ensembles were a women's tradition. The KJV's "timbrel" and modern "tambourine" add jingles that the ancient drum probably did not have. The Mekhilta says the women had packed drums when leaving Egypt, confident they would have reason to celebrate.

a: Miriam sang back to them
p: After her victory Judith leads Israel's women in a dance and sings a song that echoes Miriam's.
b: Judith, a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians include in the Old Testament, ends with a scene shaped like this one. After Judith kills the Assyrian general, the women of Israel dance, and Judith "went in front of all the people in the dance, leading all the women" (Judith 15:13). Then she sings: "Strike up for my God with tambourines!" (Judith 16:1). Like Miriam's song, hers praises God as a warrior: "For the Lord is a God who shatters wars" (Judith 16:2). The Greek Bible uses those same words in Exodus 15:3. Her song also recalls Deborah's, since the enemy falls "by a woman's hand" (Judith 16:5).

a: the wilderness of Shur
p: Shur means "wall." It may refer to Egypt's line of border forts east of the Delta.
b: Shur, "wall," lay east of Egypt, on the way Hagar fled toward home (Genesis 16:7) and on Abraham's route (Genesis 20:1). The Egyptian Story of Sinuhe (about 1900 BC) tells of a "Wall of the Ruler," built to repel Asiatics on Egypt's eastern border; Sinuhe crouched in a bush to avoid its guards. Many link the desert name with this line of forts. Numbers 33:8 calls the same region "the wilderness of Etham."

a: the LORD pointed out to him a piece of wood
t: The tree that healed the water
p: God shows (horah) Moses a tree. The rabbis called the Torah a tree; Christians saw the cross.
b: "Pointed out" is vayyorehu, from the root of torah, "teaching": the LORD "taught" him a piece of wood. The Mekhilta says some rabbis held the tree was itself bitter, so the miracle was greater, and some read it as the Torah, a "tree of life" (Proverbs 3:18). Early Christians, from Justin Martyr and Tertullian on, read the wood as the cross, which turns bitterness sweet. Ben Sira 38:5 used the story to defend medicine: "Was not water made sweet with wood?" Elisha heals water with salt in 2 Kings 2:19–22.

a: For I am the LORD, your healer
p: YHWH Rofe'kha, "the LORD your healer," is one of the compound names of God.
b: Ani YHWH rof'ekha, "I am the LORD, your healer." The verb rafa' is used of doctors (Genesis 50:2) and of God healing bodies, land and nations (2 Chronicles 7:14; Hosea 6:1). Here it promises freedom from "the sicknesses of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 7:15). The Talmud (Sanhedrin 101a) reads it as prevention: "I will not put them on you, and if I do, I am your healer." The verse is a key text for Jewish prayers for healing and for Christian healing ministry.
r: Deuteronomy 7:15; Deuteronomy 28:27; Deuteronomy 32:39; Psalm 103:3; Hosea 6:1; Mark 2:17

a: Twelve springs of water were there, and seventy palm trees
p: The twelve springs match the twelve tribes; the seventy palms match the seventy elders.
b: After the bitter water of Marah comes the oasis of Elim, "great trees." The Mekhilta and Rashi saw the numbers as signs: twelve springs for the twelve tribes and seventy palms for the seventy elders (24:1; Numbers 11:16). Origen made the stop a stage of the soul's journey: from bitterness, through teaching, to the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples (Luke 10:1). Many place Elim at Wadi Gharandel, an oasis on the west side of the Sinai peninsula.
